speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise in this House today to enter the debate. This is the first time, as a newly elected member for the constituency of Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton, that I have had an opportunity of speaking. My pride in being here as a member of parliament is somewhat tempered by humility, and the thought that I have been selected over two most worthy opponents.
Mr. Speaker, it was with interest and respect that I watched the unfolding of traditions and pageantry which marked the opening of this session and, in particular, the
3958

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
Speech from the Throne and your election to the high office which you presently hold. On behalf of my constituents and myself, I should like to congratulate you on your unanimous selection.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Your reputation as a fair, honest, impartial and just Speaker has spread far and wide to all the distant corners of this great land. I only trust that my presence in this House will not make your difficult task more difficult.
Traditionally, all forms of government by means of councils, whether they were tribal councils or the early councils in the political arenas of Greece and Rome, and through the years the evolution of the English parliamentary system, have contained the principle of allowing representatives the freedom to cast their vote as they saw fit. I am particularly pleased that the topic which we are presently debating will be decided by a free vote. In many respects it is unfortunate that the parliamentary system has evolved in such a way that a truly free vote comes so rarely. I trust that all members of the House will jealously guard and take advantage of their proper right to vote as they see fit on this topic. I trust that each member will treat with contempt any person who might try to cajole that member behind the scenes to vote otherwise than as he sees fit for the sake of some so-called party policy or party preservation. I know that members of my party will be divided on this issue and that my party is allowing each member a completely free hand to vote as he wishes.
I can only hope that every other group in this House allows a similar freedom. I hope that this is what I will see when this debate is concluded, but I expect to find it otherwise. Surely, the NDP will vote as a block in favour of this bill, belying the true representation of their constituents. On the other hand, I expect some token division in the Liberal party, but in the majority, support for the government sponsored bill as pressure is applied.
Today, we are dealing with what is frequently considered to be sentencing for what is an ultimate crime. Perhaps this is the ultimate crime in the criminal context as held in the Criminal Code of Canada, but I would like to point out that the true crime is that we are debating this topic at all at this time when tens of thousands of Canadians find themselves in an economic struggle, squeezed between unemployment and inflation. It is truly the great shame of this parliament that the government has brought in this legislation at this time. Indeed, we have spent some seven days debating this topic since the twenty-ninth parliament began, including almost one week at the very beginning, when we should have been and should now be dealing with legislation to alleviate the problems of housing, of unemployment, the abuses to the unemployment insurance fund, inflation, and the budgetary matters which have been allowed to languish by the side, languish in a barrel of unfathomable political ineptitude. Perhaps I might be permitted to refer to the section in the Criminal Code known as section 319 which deals with false pretences. Let me read briefly from the definition as follows:
A false pretence is a representation of a matter of fact in the present or past made by words or otherwise that is known by the

person who makes it to be false and that is made with a fraudulent intent to induce the person to whom it is made to act upon it.
In reading the Speech from the Throne, we note that the government's advisers have stated that the government has assigned the highest priority to two policy areas. The first listed was the economic policy to reduce unemployment, contain inflation, and to strengthen the economy generally. If that is the highest priority, then why are we dealing with capital punishment today. The government stated, first, that they wanted to expand job opportunities; second, to promote stable economic growth; third, to attain a reasonable price stability; fourth, to ensure that the regions of the country benefit through prosperity brought to all regions. It was proudly stated by the government that, having brought forth the two part program consisting of measures to provide more jobs and measures that would add fundamental strength to the economy, they would bring forth in a rush amendments to the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Customs Act, reintroduce measures announced earlier regarding screening and expand their policy on foreign take-overs, add to the social security system to assure people who cannot work, the aged, the blind and the disabled, a compassionate and equitable guaranteed income.
The entire throne speech refers to those issues which were discussed in the election campaign leading to the election on October 30. These are important issues for the majority of Canadians. Why has this legislation not been introduced? Why did we wait for 60 days to have parliament called. Why have we discussed pilotage bills, considered a lengthy Speech from the Throne which included platitudes and lollipops, had discussions on food prices, when these are only a small segment of the difficult economic problems which we face? Why was all the legislation not introduced so that it could be considered in good time, and why have we been saddled with a debate which affects, at the most, two or three people and only those people who have committed the ultimate criminal act in the context of the Criminal Code of Canada?
Truly, Mr. Speaker, the greatest criminal fraud is debating this legislation now rather than waiting to debate it at a more leisurely time. On January 26, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) stated, as reported at page 681 of Hansard, that there was no person waiting on death row. Last week, in reply to a question of mine the Solicitor General said that no person has been indicted for having committed capital murder, other than the murder of a police officer or prison guard, and has now finished the entire legal process. Any person who has committed murder since the beginning of this year has yet to go through a preliminary hearing, and finish his trial process. The indictment itself would probably be still weeks away. Surely, this debate can be held in the months ahead. If by chance a person has been convicted and is facing the death penalty, which at the moment is not a fact that person would have his sentence commuted by the government. Perhaps such sentences should be commuted until this question is settled once and for all. At least, the date of execution could be postponed.
The great criminal fraud on the Canadian public and the tens of thousands of law-abiding citizens is that they are
May 22, 1973

being made to take second place to a lengthy debate which deals with only two, three, or perhaps four convicted criminals. Somebody has his priorities sorely misplaced. A reading of the throne speech and the platitudes which were enunciated at that time, to the effect that the government was earnestly going to tackle the economic problems of the country, indicates that the government is misrepresenting itself to the people. It is misleading and deceiving the people, hoping that they will act on that deceit and misrepresentation.
Again, I point out that according to section 319 of the Criminal Code those are the ingredients which constitute false pretence. Mr. Speaker, instead of debating capital punishment the public want us to get on with the main issues at hand, the issues of inflation, wage and income control, unemployment, the unemployment insurance abuses, and perhaps even a budget. The capital punishment situation may be inconvenient to two or three people, but the government can commute their sentences. However, it cannot commute, nor does it appear willing or able, and certainly it does not appear to have the ability or knowledge on how to commute the economic squeeze in which tens of thousands of honest Canadians find themselves. Let us deal with commuting their sentences, so that they can live as they should be able to live. Dealing with this legislation now rather than with important economic matters shows a callous disregard for the good, law abiding citizens of Canada. It is an abdication of responsibility in governing this great land.
I should like to take the time to point out that the controversy which is persuading Canada on whether we should have abolition or retention has been caused by the government's ineptitude in handling criminal justice. This whole question of abolition or retention would not be as emotionally charged today if the government had not misused the parole system during the last four or five years. If the government had not allowed convicted criminals to return to society after a far too brief stay in our penitentiaries, society would feel that justice was being served. The granting of weekend passes, for days and months at a time, has eroded the confidence of the Canadian public in our system, and today the Canadian public is demanding a return of capital punishment in order to give itself a feeling of protection from that portion of society known as the criminal element.
The 70 per cent of the Canadian people who want to retain the death penalty are making a conscious decision because they have been betrayed by the easy parole granted and the favouritism shown to the criminal element of our society. If the abuse of parole and the granting of leaves to criminals had not taken place, I am convinced that a true abolitionist bill would pass, hardly challenged. Not only is a true abolitionist bill an impossibility, and so recognized by the abolitionists, but the government has had to bring in this half-baked piece of legislation knowing that the majority of the Canadian people do not want even it passed. I know from having spoken with people in the parole service over the years that the general feeling is that they cannot rehabilitate the people in prisons. They have decided, therefore, to let them out on the streets as early as possible, hoping they could rehabilitate themselves better in society. This is not what the public expects. This is not what justice demands. We must pro-
Capital Punishment
tect society. Rehabilitation ought to be and should be a foremost consideration in sentencing, but the protection of society is just as important, if not more so, and the Canadian public is demanding that.
A second fault of the Liberal administration that has been in power since 1963, and which has undermined the confidence of Canadian society in criminal justice, has been the 100 per cent commutation by the so-called royal prerogative. This House of Commons, supposedly the highest court in the land, which makes the law, has had its powers usurped by a collection of some 20 cabinet ministers who sit in the so-called treasury benches. "Treasury benches" is a peculiar term, because the occupants of those benches cannot handle the treasury but they stick their noses into areas with which they are not supposed to deal. They have usurped and by-passed the laws of the land, and by breaking the law of the land I would say that they have committed a criminal act.
The law of the land as written in this book, the Criminal Code, provides for the death penalty in section 212, but in 100 per cent of the cases the members of the Cabinet have breached that law and made a law of their own, a function which the constitution does not grant them. Certainly, there is a royal prerogative of mercy, to be used in those few cases where mercy properly should be considered. But, Mr. Speaker, mercy should not be granted in 100 per cent of the cases because then mercy loses its meaning. The royal prerogative is not a prerogative when it becomes the final court proceeding.
You cannot tell me, Mr. Speaker, and nobody else in this House could convince me, that the Queen or her representative at any time has suggested that this prerogative be used in 100 per cent of the cases. It has only been used by those members who form the cabinet of the Liberal government, because they did not have the guts or the ability to carry out the law of the land. It was not their responsibility to make themselves the court. That function is carried out by others, by a judge and jury, duly selected.
For those two reasons, the misuse of parole and the misuse of the royal prerogative, the government has now caused society's great concern and has forced itself into an untenable position. This bill is neither fish nor fowl. It is not an abolitionist bill. The Solicitor General is an abolitionist. He has stated so. Even though he is an avowed abolitionist, he knows that he cannot successfully achieve that objective, and therefore is trying to put in the thin end of the wedge by means of this legislation. I say to him that if he is a true abolitionist let him bring in an abolitionist bill and get a true reflection of the feelings of the elected representatives in this House.
For many years I was an abolitionist. I regret, in many ways, that I am not one any longer. I am not voting against this bill because I know that 70 per cent of my constituents want to retain the death penalty. I am voting against this bill because I know that society as a whole feels cheated, and feels a need of protection. I will vote against this bill at all stages until we have adequately given society its proper right to experience a sense of security. I hope that in the next few years the royal prerogative will not be misused, that the parole system and leaves of absence will not be abused, and that this matter of abolition or retention can come up again after
3960

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
society has experienced a period of security. At that time, I will be voting for the abolition of the death penalty.
I have no qualms about the loss of the life of a criminal. Mr. Speaker, we pay lip service to the loss of thousands of people each year through war and on the highways, and now we are trying to pay more lip service to that person who has taken a life than we do the many law-abiding citizens who lose their lives by accident. Life is important and it is precious-probably the most precious thing in this world but only to the person who possesses that life and to those persons who are near and dear to him or her. But nobody can convince me that the life of an unknown person is precious to me, as I did not know that person, so let us not pretend that this bill and abolition is the godly thing to do to protect the most precious thing in the world-life. Mr. Speaker, I am not convinced that we have to treat a person who has caused the death of another person in a criminal act any better than other criminals. It is only some philosophical moralistic burbling which causes certain people to shrink and shirk their proper duty.
Before taking my seat, I should like to inform this House, briefly that I have had experience in criminal law. For three years I prosecuted criminals in Ottawa, the capital city. I have prosecuted bank robbers who have committed five and six robberies and it is all there on their record. They are known as professionals. They call themselves and consider themselves professional robbers. On each occasion they have armed themselves with a sawed-off shotgun, a pistol, machine gun, a submachine gun, automatic rifle and with two or three companions entered a bank or the premises of their intended victim, after having planned for 10, 30 and sixty days in minute and complete detail every step that they were going to take. They have armed themselves, Mr. Speaker, with the full knowledge that they may use those weapons to take a life, and in most instances they are the types of people who would sooner shoot than give you the time of day.
I have no respect whatsoever for those people. They commit an armed robbery and are caught. They are given five years on their first attempt and they are out in 18 months. They are caught again, they get seven years and they are out in IVi years. Perhaps they do not get caught for the next two or three times, but ultimately they are found out. Then, they are tried on two or three armed robberies at the one time and this time they are sentenced to ten or eleven years, so they are out in three or four years. Finally, in the course of a robbery they kill someone because that person happens to be interfering with their criminal act of robbing. When a criminal has such a record why should we give him special consideration? I think, Mr. Speaker, I would rather have special consideration given to the law-abiding public. Then, on the other hand, I have dealt with the criminals who were just sadists, and I would like to deal with one case in particular which gives some indication of whether or not the death penalty is a deterrent.
On January 3, 1969 at the end of the festive season, two couples, one couple in each car, were minding their own business and driving from Ottawa to Almonte. Three sadistic, brutal, vicious young men followed them for a

period of what must have been 15 or 20 minutes or longer, then flagged down the cars pretending they were stranded at the side of the road. Then, having had the opportunity for 15 or 20 minutes of thinking what they were about to do, they cold bloodedly killed two men, the heads of families, while their wives watched, cowering underneath the dashboard of their car. They pumped bullet after bullet into those people, themselves unarmed, who were just good Samaritans stopping to help somebody stranded at the side of the road. After having had an opportunity to consider what they were doing their course of action for 20 minutes, they deliberately murdered two men. The names of the three murderers were David John Brault, David Dwyer and Donald Phillion. It became known as the Carp murders. Now, the government and its advisers want us to vote in favour of those people.
Let me take this case one step further. I have here a partial copy of the transcript of the court proceedings, uncontradicted, of the preliminary hearing. The murderers went their separate ways after they had committed this act. One of them, David Dwyer, went to Windsor where he was tracked down by a police officer in the basement of a house. On page 251 of the transcript of the preliminary hearing, in examination in chief when giving identification, Mr. Chippit was asked:
Q. What name did you know him by at that time?
A. Dwyer, David Dwyer.
Q. When you saw him, how was he dressed?
A. He had a brown jacket on; hair blond and he had what appeared to be a .22 calibre rifle pointed at my head.
And a little later:
Q. How long was this weapon?
A. It was sawed off, cut down.
On page 252, continuing the examination in chief of Mr. Chippit:
Q. Was there any struggle?
A. No struggle at all, sir.
Q. Did Dwyer say anything at this point?
A. He just walked out very nonchalantly. After I said "Drop it", he said all right and walked out.
And a little later:
Q. Was there any conversation on the way to the station?
A. Yes there was.
Q. What was the conversation?
A. You are talking about conversation in the car after we left the scene?
Q. Yes.
A. That is correct.
Q. Yes?
A. The conversation was, if I remember, we were talking; it was brought up in regard-we were talking of an armed robbery in the city of Windsor. I stated, well, this time don't worry about it, and he-
Referring to Dwyer.
-said, "No, this is a bad city to pull a robbery." He says, "I have had better luck other places."
Q. This was Dwyer; is that correct?
A. This is correct.
Further, on page 254, continuing examination in chief:
Q. -What was the accused's attitude during the time you were in his company?
May 22, 1973

A. He was very nonchalant, sir. He asked me for a cigarette, and then when we were leaving the scene, or the car was leaving the scene in the police car W.H.Q.
Q. W.H.Q.?
A. Headquarters.
Q. Did you get the cigarette?
A. I looked at him and said, "You guys are crazy; just had a gun to my head and now you want a cigarette.'' He said-
This is referring to Mr. Dwyer.
-"I would not shoot you, I would hang for that."
That is the uncontradicted evidence of the preliminary hearing. Those men pleaded guilty and were sentenced for non-capital murder. As indicated, the Windsor police came to where Mr. Dwyer was staying in the basement, where he had his rifle in his hand, having a little target practice in the basement. When the police officer came down the man pointed the loaded rifle at his head but he did not shoot the police officer. As indicated in that transcript, ten minutes later when he was disarmed he asked the police officer for the cigarette and the police officer said "Man, you must be crazy, ten minutes ago you were in a position to shoot me and now you are asking me a favour; you want a cigarette". This person who had already killed two ordinary citizens for which he must have known he was not going to hang, then stated "I would not shoot you, I would hang for that." He did not hurt the police officer, because for that he would have had to hang. You say the death penalty is not a deterrent. There is proof. It was a deterrent for that criminal in that situation. If it was a deterrent for that person, it may be a deterrent for many others. I hope, as I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation brought forward at this time will be defeated.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it clear from the outset that, based on the evidence I have read and studied, I am in favour of abolishing capital punishmment in Canada. I, therefore, support the present bill as a compromise which extends abolition for five more years, except in the case of the murder of a police officer or a prison guard. I take this stand, Mr. Speaker, despite the survey that I sent to my constituents in January, in which 73 per cent of the over 4,000 people who replied indicated that they were in favour of retaining the death penalty. I know it would be politically safe to go along with them in what I consider a sincere decision on their part. But, Mr. Speaker, this is to be a free vote, and it is a vote of conscience. On the basis, of the evidence of my studies, I could not, with a clear conscience, support capital punishment.
I have listened to speeches in this House on capital punishment and read letters from individuals across Canada. What has struck me has been the legitimate concern of the public for its safety; but what disturbs me about much of this public concern is the lack of research and the undue emotionalism on which many of the arguments, both pro and con, are predicated. As I see it, if one is to argue for or against capital punishment, one can do so on three grounds: Whether or not the death penalty is a deterrent to crime; how society is to be protected from a repetition of capital offences by convicted criminals, and this of course involves parole policy; and, finally, to what degree should society seek the punishment or rehabilita-
Capital Punishment
tion of the criminal. I should like now to put forth arguments on each of these three grounds, which I believe lead one who employs reason and logic to support the abolitionist position.
The most common argument used by those who are in favour of retaining capital punishment is that it serves as an effective deterrent to murder. Indeed, in response to my questionnaire on that question, 52 per cent of my constituents who replied thought that capital punishment was an effective deterrent. Common sense, it is argued by retentionists, tells us that people are afraid of death. Soldiers on the battlefield fear it, you fear it, Mr. Speaker, and I fear it. Likewise, it is argued that the potential murderer will not commit the crime of murder because of fear of execution. Yet does not common sense tell us that if we drive recklessly on the highway, without using a seat belt, we run the risk of a fatal accident? Does the fear of death stop the carnage on our highways? Doctors and medical science tell us that cigarette smoking contributes to death by lung cancer. Surely this warning, coupled with reason, would induce us to stop smoking; yet more people are smoking today than ever before.
The so-called common sense approach to the deterrent factor of death needs to be reassessed. A superficial analysis of this problem has no place in this debate. Common sense may tell us one thing, but reason tells us another. Reason, based on case study analysis, tells us that for many criminals the determining factor is not the fear of death or punishment but whether or not the criminal will be caught. The criminal commits the crime on the assumption he will not be caught. I can think of no better illustration of this than that in nineteenth century England, when pickpocketing was a capital offence and pickpockets were executed at public hangings, pickpockets made their greatest hauls at public executions when the eyes of the crowd were turned upward to the hangman's noose. Also, in nineteenth century England a chaplain who conducted 167 men to the gallows related that 164 of them had attended at public executions. Where was the deterrent?
The professional killers of organized crime, the political assassin or the man who commits homicide in the course of another crime, are not deterred by the death penalty. The professional killer is not deterred because murder is his job and, as he is skilled, he does not expect to be caught. The political assassin is not deterred, because to him the cause is the be all and end all, and he is ready to die for it. The thief who commits murder in the course of a robbery is not deterred, because in the majority of cases he does not plan to kill but does so as an immediate reaction to avoid capture.
According to my studies, such criminals account for only about 29 per cent of all murders in Canada, 71 per cent of murders in Canada being committed as a result of domestic quarrels or arguments with a friend. In these crimes, alcohol is often a contributing factor. Study after study has shown that the murder of a relative or friend, or the homicide committed by a drunk during a fight or by a mentally deranged person, is a murder committed on the spur of the moment, without premeditattion. It is committed in a fit of passion. The person in such a state of emotional hysteria thinks only of killing. He does not

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
reflect calmly on the fear of capital punishment. Capital punishment has not deterred criminals in the past; nor will it do so if it is reintroduced.
Canada abolished the death penalty in 1967, except for the murder of police and prison officials. Did this result in an increase in the frequency of murder in Canada? The important word here is, frequency. The number of murders increased, but this increase was part of the general increase in over-all crime, that is, in crimes of all categories. What is important is the rate of increase in homicides. The detailed and comprehensive study by Dr. Fattah of McGill University shows that the increase in criminal homicide is the lowest among all crimes of violence. Also, there is no indication of any consistent trend in the rate of homicide. The rate fluctuates from year to year. Indeed, the largest increase in the murder rate in Canada since 1964 occurred in the year before abolition, not in the year after. Nor has the retention of the death penalty as punishment for the murder of police or prison officials proved to be an effective deterrent. The largest number of police murders took place in 1962, when capital punishment was in effect. Two murderers were hanged that year. The murder of police has been on the increase since 1967, despite the fact that it is still a capital offence. Research shows that the murder rate of policemen is substantially similar in abolitionist and retentionist countries having the same social and economic conditions. Reason, Mr. Speaker, must convince us that capital punishment is not a deterrent to murder. We cannot retain hanging in Canada on the ground that it will reduce the homicide rate in this country.
The second ground for discussing this whole issue, as I mentioned, is, how is society to be protected from a repetition of capital offences by convicted criminals? It seems to me that much of the public's concern about the crime rate has to do with present-day parole procedures, the laxity of which in certain cases has led to the parole of dangerous criminals who have committed crimes while on parole. In my opinion, the way to alleviate this threat to the public's safety is not to parole certain types of criminals where rehabilitation is risky; for example, the sexual offender or the psychotic. Perhaps we should provide that the sentence of life imprisonment means the rest of a person's natural life in the case of a murderer involved in organized crime or a professional killer. The whole parole procedure should be reassessed and a more cautious approach should be taken in the matter of paroles. The public has a right to be concerned about our parole policy. I share their concern. However, I do not wish to dwell on this because I believe it is an ancillary issue to the real one we are debating in Bill C-2.
The other question before us, aside from the deterrent factor and the protection of society, is the degree to which we seek punishment and/or rehabilitation. Much of the debate has centered around the argument of a life for a life; he who murders should not expect mercy. I am perplexed that those who advocate capital punishment on the grounds that the murderer, because he has committed a most heinous crime, should be punished accordingly, do not carry their argument to its logical conclusion. If a man commits a brutal murder and if it is vengeance they want,

is not hanging too good to him? Why not make him suffer as much as the victim? Why not revert to the medieval practice of torture before death?
We do not have to go back as far as the Middle Ages for an example of how this could be done. I refer to the case of Jean Calas in France in 1761. This event occurred in an age to which historians refer as the period of enlightenment; today, the age of reason. Jean Calas, a 64 year old Protestant merchant in Toulouse was falsely accused of strangling his son to prevent him from becoming a convert to Roman Catholicism. The public were outraged and wanted vengeance. He was tried, convicted of murder and sentenced to death. Calas appealed his case and, in order to elicit the truth, the court ordered that he be tortured until he confessed. Here is a description of what took place:
The decision was appealed to the Parlement of Toulouse, which appointed a panel of thirteen judges. Sixty-three additional witnesses were heard. All the hostile evidence was hearsay. . . . The final decision condemned only the father. No one explained how a man sixty-four years old, unaided, could have overcome and strangled his mature son. The court hoped that Calas, under torture, would confess. He was subjected to the question ordinaire: his arms and legs were stretched until they were pulled from their sockets. He was repeatedly exhorted to confess; he repeatedly affirmed that Marc Antoine had committed suicide. After half an hour's rest he was put to the question extraordinaire; fifteen pints of water were poured down his throat; he still protested his innocence; fifteen further pints were forced into him, swelling his body to twice its normal size; he still maintained his innocence. He was allowed to expel the water. Then he was taken to a public square before the cathedral; he was laid upon a cross; an executioner, with eleven blows of an iron bar, broke each of his limbs in two places; the old man, calling upon Jesus Christ, proclaimed his innocence. After two hours of agony he was strangled. The corpse was bounded to a stake and burned (March 10, 1762).
If we carried out executions like that today we could, according to those who favour capital punishment, not only deter would-be murderers by the spectacle but satisfy our blood-lust for vengeance as well. I believe that Canadians are more civilized than that. Just as we no longer hang children for petty theft, as we did in Canada 150 years ago, so let us follow the civilized practice of the United Kingdom, Australia, Italy, Sweden, Finland, Austria, Germany and many other countries and abolish capital punishment. There is enough brutalization of society in our 20th century world without state murder.
If we are civilized, surely we should stress rehabilitation rather than vengeance. Where rehabilitiation fails or is impossible, let the punishment be life imprisonment, that is for the rest of the murderer's natural life. Let us not ignore the preventative aspect of the question. I have yet to see a baby born a murderer. We must work to eliminate these socio-economic environments which breed crime and distort human behaviour. If we put more effort into cleaning up slums, reducing unemployment and poverty, mending broken homes, tackling the problems of alcoholism and drug abuse and bringing in tighter gun controls, we will do more to reduce the crime rate in Canada than by throwing the criminals into jail or conducting them to the gallows.
I have tried to explain why capital punishment cannot be justified on the ground that it is a deterrent to crime. I have tried to show that society can be protected from the convicted criminal repeating a serious offence by a more
May 22, 1973

judicious parole system and tighter prison security. I have emphasized that rehabilitation is more important than retribution. I urge the members of this House and all Canadians not to regress to the barbaric practices of our ancestors. Surely, in a civilized and forward looking society, the philosophy of an eye for an eye or of brutal blood lust has no place. Man prides himself on his ability to reason. We pride ourselves on the rule of law that we have developed down through the ages. As Filippo Grammatica wrote in his treatise Pena de Morte, and I quote:
If the law of man does not allow murder, if murder has neither a human nor a social function and hence it is not lawful, if it is ill-advised, if it is immoral, if it is anti-aesthetic, how can it become lawful, moral, aesthetic and functional for a particular offence?
I suggest it can only become lawful if we forgo reason and regress to emotionalism or a primitive desire for revenge. Boris Pasternack wrote in his novel Dr. Zhivago, and I quote:
If the beast in man could be held down by threats-any kind of threat, whether in jail or retribution after death-then the highest emblem of humanity would be the lion tamer in the circus with his whip, not the Prophet who sacrificed himself.
It was that Prophet who, while hanging on the cross, forgave his murderers and taught us to pray "forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us". It is my sincere hope that, nearly 2,000 years later, we shall finally learn this lesson and abolish capital punishment in Canada.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are back again today on Bill C-2 and we see speakers rise one after the other, some of them wanting to retain capital punishment, others wanting to abolish it. What surprises me is precisely the fact that Bill C-2 in no way offers a choice between retention and abolition of capital punishment but is a request on the part of the government to postpone the decision on that issue.
We have arguments from both sides. Some hon. members say that capital punishment can diminish or reduce acts of violence in Canada; on the other hand, other hon. members on the basis of statistics, probably the same, say that it is not the solution to the problem. But everybody forgets that in the first place the government is not trying hard enough as far as the administration is concerned to minimize the incidence of murders or other offences. It is not doing enough to rightly help the population to live decently and it can be seen when studies are made in prisons that a good number of criminals come from low-income groups.
Theoretically, arguments and standpoints are easy to put forward but in reality, practically nothing is being done to control the causes of crime.
I read in the speech made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and I quote:
Underlying all of these characteristics, which make our society so human, is the belief by Canadians that in such a social system they can flourish and pursue their lives free from fear of lawless elements.
Capital Punishment
I wonder whether the Prime Minister would say the same thing had he been attacked as some bank employees are, or had a member of his family been attacked as members of other Canadian families are? We realize that philosophizing is easy, but that concrete action is much more difficult. I resume my quotation from the Prime Minister's speech:
Jailbreaks will be dealt with as the enquiries and the Solicitor General recommend.
I remember that on February 9, when I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) if he had read the report on the Pinel Institute inquiry on a psychiatrist who was implicated in murderer Real Chartrand's case, the Solicitor General told me he had not. We are still waiting for his reply today, still waiting for a statement on the position of the government that part of the problem might be solved before abolishing the death penalty: first things must come first. The first thing the government should do is ensure the well being of society. The second, when citizens have broken the law, been caught and imprisoned, before anything else is to ensure the security of the places of detention.
No need to discuss the problem very long. We only need to read the latest newspapers to realize that there have been 34 escapes. Our prisons have become sieves. Is this the attitude of a law-abiding individual? Absolutely not. What steps are we taking? Inquiries! Inquiries leading where? Nowhere. This is exactly what happened after the inquiry allegedly made by the Solicitor General: no result. The psychiatrist is probably still in a position to parole criminals. Nothing is going to be done about that, yet the government is ready to help those who live on the fringe of society or of the law. As a matter of fact, the right hon. Prime Minister declared, and I quote:
. . . the administration of criminal justice in Canada. No ingredient in this process is less important than any other. None can be ignored by society; none will be ignored by the government.
However, because of the lack of action on the part of the government people are allowed to leave prisons, either as parolees, or as escapees-as is the case now-because of the inefficient prison administration. This is given as much importance as helping society.
I am seriously wondering. What does the government intend to do in this instance? Speaking of prisons, the right hon. Prime Minister said, and I am quoting:
Society intended them in the first instance to be secure. And this government intends to ensure that they are secure.
But what measures is it taking? Inquiries, again and again. Then, Members of Parliament are left to discuss the
advisability of delaying or not the decision concerning capital punishment.
This whole system or argumentation is worthless because it does not guarantee prison security, it does not enable society to be sure that prisoners will remain in prison. And as a justification, the Prime Minister adds, and I quote:
And 1 say, too, with all the earnestness at my command that prisoners who have broken jail or who have exploited temporary leave and other humanitatian reforms-and who by doing so have placed these programs in jeopardy for thousands of other prisoners-

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
The government prefers helping prisoners to helping society. If some prisoners escape, they are recaptured and kept under surveillance, and people are sorry that they restricted other prisoners' freedom. One remembers the case of a prisoner who escaped, disappeared while visiting the Salon de la femme. How many law-abiding citizens are able to visit important functions such as the Salon de la femme, or go to hockey or football matches, as prisoners are allowed to? Can it be that the government prefers to help prisoners and maintain their standard of living, whatever their crimes, to the detriment of the rest of the population?
This is the funniest part of it all, and I shall end on this: the thing that surprises me most, of all the attitudes we see here in the House, is that those who do not want to take a stand, those who want to allow killers to go on killing, are the first to defend the right of abortion, the right to kill a child in its mother's womb. But they refuse the right to punish those who have killed a person. There is a double standard in the minds of these people.
Mr. Speaker, as long as the government will not consider different steps to be taken, rationally rather than emotionally, that is to say, as I said earlier, to secure the welfare of the people; as long as the government will not be assured that criminals will really remain in jail; as long as the government will not have statistics on the chances of rehabilitating some prisoners, namely those who have committed two or three murders and were allowed to return to society and commit another one before being put back in jail-which is precisely something about which society does not feel secure and in which it does not want to interfere-I suggest that we must at least create a feeling of fear among criminals by retaining capital punishment.
As a matter of fact, as soon as the government has passed legislation which will enable the Canadian people to feel secure and not to fear, whenever they are walking along the main streets of big cities, to be killed by some frightening person in the course of a holdup, we will feel better.
Criminals are ready to defend themselves but is society in a position to defend itself against such individuals? I am prepared to believe that statistics are of little meaning and that it is possible to use them to support opposite views but once again they do not in the least demonstrate the necessity of abolishing capital punishment now.
If the government by adopting measures-and I repeat it-guarantees to society the benefits I mentioned earlier, namely the welfare of the population, the security of jails and the rehabilitation of inmates, then it will be in a position to think of abolishing capital punishment.
This is briefly what I had to say today on capital punishment. Once more, I regret that Bill C-2 is nothing else than a measure to abolish or maintain capital punishment. Indeed, it is nothing else but a measure aimed at delaying this decision for quite a while.
Mr. Speaker, before voting on this bill, we should take our time to think about the pros and cons and above all to permit the government to act more efficiently in other areas than it seems prepared to do for deferring a decision such as that required by Bill C-2.

This is what I had to say and, once more, I hope hon. members will take an honest decision on such a question before the vote.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once more Bill C-2 has been presented to us for debate. To me, it seems stupid and ridiculous to waste the time of this House debating this bill when there is much more important business before the House which is of the greatest concern to the people of Canada. Parliament has been sitting for over four months now, and while some good legislation has been passed there is a great deal more waiting in the wings which is of vital importance, legislation that certainly should have been presented and passed into law by this time.
During the earlier part of the session when the debate took place I believe there were 35 eloquent and passionate speeches made both for and against capital punishment. The news media have polled about 91 members of the House and, with their expertise, have decided that the vote is going to be close. I believe only 10 members are wavering and have not yet made up their minds which way they intend to vote. I suppose it could be said by a great many of the members that just debating and debating the bill is an exercise in futility. We could quote the old statement: "My mind is made up, so don't confuse me with the facts".
We already know from the many eloquent speeches and quotations that anything that will be said from now on will only be repetition. I understand the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that as long as he is Prime Minister no one will hang. That statement was made a couple of weeks ago, but I believe he refuted it a little later. But regardless of that, since he has been Prime Minister, and in fact since 1962, there has been no capital punishment carried out. This is proof that this bill cannot be considered a high priority item and could very well be put at the bottom of the pile.
I understand that in Canada there is one lawyer for every 1,653 persons. However, the ratio is much greater in this House; I believe there are 63 lawyers among the 264 members. In fact, there could be even more, since some members who are qualified lawyers have another profession and may be differently classified. But with due respect to this august and most learned group, these legal people go on at great length speaking in terms and in language that the ordinary layman, especially the new member of parliament, does not understand. They speak about de jure, de facto and so on. I see no reason why they cannot speak plain, ordinary English so most of us can understand. Then, when these members send copies of their speeches in Hansard to their constituents, they will be able to understand it, too.
To get down to the bare bones of the case, I wish to state my position in no uncertain terms. I believe in some form of capital punishment as a deterrent, in the final analysis. If I decide to walk across this chamber, pull out a gun and shoot the Prime Minister in a cold-blooded and calculating manner, and if I am proven sane, I feel there is no other alternative for me but capital punishment. However, I am

not in favour of hanging. I think it is a gruesome and terrible form of capital punishment. Neither am I too impressed with the electric chair or the gas chamber. I feel some form of humane capital punishment is more appropriate, such as administering a drug which would be painless.
As we all know, statistics can be quoted one way or the other, depending on the views of the speaker. It is my belief that certain types of cold-blood and calculated murder can only be dealt with in one way. The dastardly murder of Pierre Laporte, a cold-blooded, premeditated murder, was a murder no one could deny fell into this category. We are all aware that the great majority of murders are crimes of passion, and there is no question that such murderers, if found guilty, will be sentenced to prison terms of varying duration. However, there are certain types of fiendish murder, such as rape killings, molesting and murdering of small children, which are so terrible and horrible that the greatest punishment must be available if circumstances warrant.
I am aware that many of the persons who commit this sort of murder are of unsound mind and on a great many occasions are committed to an institution. I have listened with great respect to many previous speakers, both at the present time and during the earlier debate, and in fact re-read a great many of the speeches that were made, and I was most impressed with them. However, whether we like it or not, we are living in a violent society. We have a great many depraved individuals running around loose who are potential murderers. We also have potential murderers running around loose as well as convicted murderers.
There are a great many cold-blooded gangsters who at this very moment in all probability, are plotting crimes which may lead eventually to the killing of some innocent victims. These certainly are not crimes of passion or crimes which are committed on the spur of the moment. This is the type of crime for which there should be the death penalty, if circumstances prove it is warranted. We have heard statistics quoted by previous speakers. While they concede that the number of crimes is up, they believe there are mitigating circumstances. The latest figures provided by Statistics Canada show that the number of violent crimes of murder has increased 113 per cent. Again, let me emphasize that I would recommend the most humane form of capital punishment available. This, I think, could be provided through an amendment. A great many speakers on the abolitionist side have gone into the gory details of hanging. They have resurrected ancient history by going back a thousand years.
One hon. member a short while ago cited a murder, and the terrible punishment involved, in the year 1762. Hon. members have gone into the matter in great detail. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) cited cases. I believe he went back to the time of William the Conqueror. Mr. Speaker, we are intelligent people. We are talking about capital punishment in this day and age, 1973. It is not necessary for us to refer to the gory details of ancient times or as far back as 1,000 years. This makes very good reading and makes cold chills run up and down the spines of many people. It starts them thinking that probably capital punishment should be abolished. Every
Capital Punishment
day members of the police forces risk their lives trying to capture and imprison criminals. Then, they watch in dismay and anger while the courts juggle sentences that do everything except fit the crime. The more dangerous the criminal is the more protection the law seems to give him or her in attempting to evade prison, utterly ignoring the victim or possible future victims as soon as the criminal is loose again.
We seem to be going overboard in this permissive age in giving the greatest consideration to those who evade the law rather than to those who are the victims of the criminals. Several hon. members have forwarded questionnaires to their constituents. A great majority of these have been returned overwhelmingly in favour of the retention of capital punishment. Surveys taken by newspapers have also verified this. A survey taken by the Ottawa Journal last fall, with additions added to it, verified that over 90 per cent of the people were in favour of retention. Certainly, these 90 per cent could not be classified as morbid, vengeful people who have no compassion. I am aware that among younger people there are more in favour of abolition, but still the majority, the population favours some form of retention. I have received many letters from citizens in my riding outlining their views. The great majority favour retention of capital punishment. They also point out that this should not be restricted to the killing of policemen or prison guards, which would be the case if this particular bill should be enacted.
This brings up the point mentioned by previous speakers that this bill is neither flesh nor fowl. It is neither a bill for abolition nor for retention. There are, I believe six clergymen who are members of the opposition. I believe we should listen more closely to what is said by the six clergymen in this august House. A poll of these six members shows that three are in favour of abolition and three are in favour of retention. Certainly these distinguished and honoured members of this House should not be classified as vengeful people. I believe there is one clergyman on the government side who, I imagine, would be an abolitionist.
I should like to comment on that great moulder of public opinion, the news media. I believe a poll of this group would probably show the great majority to be in favour of total abolition. Therefore, it follows that editorial stories and news reports are slanted quite often in such a way as to portray the position of the writer. Cartoons show the scaffold and noose in the chilling dawn. On Tuesday morning of last week, I was up bright and early listening to the CTV news program "A M." which I believe came on at eight o'clock. The reporter was giving news of the world. Then, he casually mentioned that the capital punishment bill would be debated on that day, which it was. Certainly, that statement was not biased in any way. However, behind him there was a cartoon denoting the noose and the scaffold. If that is not biased reporting by the CTV news media, then I do not know what is.
The Toronto Star some while ago made some comments on this bill and included a cartoon with a grey coloured chilly dawn, a scaffold and a rope. This makes the situation as gruesome as possible. Why should the cartoon not depict the sordidness of the murder of a young woman or child rather than this. Weekend magazine had quite an
3966

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
article on hanging. Again, however, this is a misnomer in a way. This bill is called the hanging bill. It is a bill to retain capital punishment. It will enable the cabinet to reprieve the sentence, as the have done in the past.
Mr. Speaker, last week we listened with great interest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party when they spoke in sequence. As we know, they are all abolitionists. The Prime Minister cited the position of the government as well as the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and voiced his opinion. Our own leader voiced his opinion. The eloquent and knowledgeable or know-it-all Leader of the New Democratic Party stated his opinion as if it were the Papal edict and the only one which should be considered. He stated he was an abolitionist. He conceded that the people in his riding were in favour of retention but that they probably did not know what they were talking about. He went on at great length to point out that this House should make the decision. Naturally, he was putting across his case for total abolition.
It has been emphasized during this debate by those who are putting across the case for abolition that those who are retentionists must be acting primarily on the basis of vengeance or on the basis that capital punishment is a deterrent. However, this idea of vengeance is really pleaded in a most vehement way. And, of course, they cite vengeful forms of capital punishment in use throughout the past 100 years.
There is one other thing which we must emphasize, and this has been brought out time and time again. We speak about compassion and mercy. It seems to me that all the compassion and mercy is for the criminal or the murderer. There does not seem to be too much consideration or compassion for the victim or for his loved ones who are left behind. They do not seem to be considered. It is the opinion of the abolitionists that no matter how depraved the criminal is, he can certainly be rehabilitated and put back into society. I think we are all aware that there are certain individuals for whom redemption is not possible and, therefore, they should be eliminated from society in the most painless way possible.
The ordinary man and woman have lost their faith in justice and those in authority, seem to be on the side of the criminal. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) suggested in the earlier debate that a referendum be held at the next general election. I am certainly willing to stand up here and vote as my conscience tells me. If it is the opinion that there should be a general referendum, then possibly there is merit in this suggestion. However, let me tell you that it seems to me the great majority of those who favour abolition are diametrically opposed to any referendum being held, and with good cause. They know only too well that a referendum will show that people are overwhelmingly in favour of retention, and we have these figures, 70 per cent, to put it at its lowest, or 90 per cent to put it at its highest, to prove that is the case.
Capital punishment for the criminal who has committed first degree murder must be put back on the statute books and enforced. Beyond the shadow of a doubt, justice must

not only be done but must be seen to be done. A great many members of this House have been quoting learned people and experienced penologists. They have quoted Dr. Fattah, Dr. Thinner, and so forth. It might be a good idea to read into the record some of the comments of just plain, ordinary citizens. I have some letters here. One of them reads:
Dear Mr. Darling: We wish to inform you we are against the government continuing its policy of abolishing the death penalty.

speechtext:
Mad dog murderers should be disposed of permanently, not stored up in the pen. This means not only for the killing of policemen and prison guards, but for any other person. The entire population must receive this benefit. It is not the question of a deterrent, it is the question these murderers mut pay with their life-as simple as that. Politicians must be virile, strong people, look the matter squarely in the face. If any of their family or close friends were murdered, they would be the first to raise a fuss. As an ex-mountie, I, like other policemen, are sick of the pampering of criminals. No wonder the country is weak and divided . ..
And he goes on.
The following was conveyed to me by telephone by a merchant in the town of Huntsville:
One of your voters wishes you to know that I have been talking to hundreds of people re capital punishment and they want it reinstated 99 per cent.
Then, he said: "Are you in favour of it?" Here is another letter which reads:
We, the undersigned, wish to express to you our desire for the restoration of capital punishment for the crime of murder.
I could go on and on, and read all these into the record. These letters are from God-fearing citizens. We must forget about this inane compassion and mercy toward premeditated killers. This House will have to decide. I know the vote will be close, and I know the people of Canada are looking very closely at how this will turn out. When the time comes, I will be casting my vote for the retention of capital punishment. Let me hope that if I am privileged to be in the House for a number of years I will be here long enough to see the time when Canadians will be able to abolish capital punishment, but we are in a society now that does not warrant it.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
