speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate with some reluctance only because I want to see the bill sent to committee at the earliest possible moment, and I do not want to prolong the discussion. But I do hope that having reached committee stage certain amendments might be considered. For while I support the bill in principle and shall vote for it, I have two major reservations. First, being in favour of the total abolition of capital punishment, I find it illogical to make exceptions for any one group, be they prison guards, police officers or heads of state. Others have dealt with this
May 22, 1973

aspect of illogicality, and I shall not repeat their reservations which I share. Second, I do not believe that we need another five year trial period, and I shall return to that point later. Also, I regret that this debate on the retention or the abolition of capital punishment-for that is really what we are debating-is taking place at a time when the viability and effectiveness of both the penitentiary system and the parole services have been called into question by an increasingly sceptical and resentful public.
Recurring prison breakouts have become synonymous in the minds of many Canadians with the present debate on capital punishment to the extent where some people are quite convinced that all inmates are guilty of murder. I think we have a responsibility to delineate the differences in these major areas of concern, that is between capital punishment and reforms to the penitentiary and parole systems, in order to correct the distortion and the confusion that now abound.
We are all primarily concerned with the protection of society from the crime of murder. That goes without saying. There is no one here who does not consider the protection of the public to take precedence over every other concern. The question that naturally follows is whether or not capital punishment is a protective measure. It is, only if it can be clearly proven that it has a deterrent value. But the statistical evidence for such a conclusion is lacking.
I have heard statistics used to support the abolition of the death penalty and I have heard them used to support the retention of the death penalty. One statistic I have not heard used is that there have been only two murder repeats in Canada since 1897. Professor Fattah's study, which has been referred to repeatedly in this debate, shows that murder as a component of violent crime has risen less than other crimes of violence in recent years. His conclusions firmly state that "the increase in criminal homicide in Canada during recent years cannot be attributed to the suspension of capital punishment." He rejects the argument that capital punishment is a significant deterrent.
Other studies based on research done in the United States where, until a recent United States Supreme Court decision, individual states had the right to establish a death penalty or not for whatever crime they deemed necessary, have shown, (a) that the death penalty has had no discernible effect on homicide death rates; (b) that abolitionist states have fewer killings of police officers than states with the death penalty, and (c), that a comparison of homicide rates in states that have abolished the death penalty, before and after abolition, shows that abolition did not give rise to significant change in homicide rates. In Canada murder rates have increased less than many other indictable offences. Since the abolition of the past five years has resulted in no significant increases in murder rates, we can probably predict with some degree of accuracy that a return to capital punishment would not significantly reduce homicide rates.
But the area to which I would like specifically to direct my attention is rehabilitation rather than the contentious, and to this point unresolveable, argument about deter-
Capital Punishment
rence. And I must admit candidly that I find it difficult to discuss this or any other aspect of the capital punishment debate with dispassionate objectivity.
Having been involved in voluntary work in the prison system, having spent long hours in discussion with people sentenced for murder, having seen the work and effort put forward by individuals to rehabilitate themselves, all make it impossible for me to approach this debate impersonally. And I must say in this connection that having seen what some individuals have accomplished in the way of rehabilitation, my response to them is one of admiration. On occasion, I have accompanied inmates on their day out, have had women sentenced for murder visit my home while on special passes, and I have seen them go on to earn their parole and re-establish themselves in their communities. I know businessmen and community workers, in this city and in others, who were once convicted of murder and who are now contributing members of society.
There are other individuals currently in our penal institutions who have utilized their time to upgrade their skills and their education-yes, people who have committed murder, but who have spent long years working through correspondence to a university degree in social work, in law, in the arts and in other fields. And their acquired knowledge is being used to benefit their fellow inmates.
I mention these people only to express my firm belief in rehabilitation. These people, on whom society might have inflicted capital punishment, remained instead to contribute to that society. You may ask, but what about their victims and the relatives of their victims? What about compassion for them? I admit that I have never known the relatives of a person who has been murdered. But my stand in favour of abolition would in no way be changed were I to do so, for execution of a murderer would not restore the victim to life, nor would it comfort or solace his family and friends. It makes no sense to me that one protects the sanctity of human life by taking a life. If we consider that an act of violence, hanging, is necessary to avenge an earlier act of violence, murder, then surely we are saying that our society is bankrupt in its struggle to reach new levels of humanitarianism.
I cannot rid my mind of the possibility of mistakes being made in our judicial system. Neither our judges nor juries, like all other human beings, are without their imperfections. In this connection just the other day I read a letter in the Ottawa Citizen as follows:
We have heard quite a few times about the date of the last hanging in Canada. How much do we know about the first one? While reading in the Kingston Public Library about the town (or village as it was then) of Bath, Ontario, in 1795, I found it was there the first hanging took place. The man was charged with stealing a watch and later was proved to have been innocent.
That was our first public hanging in this part of the country.
I wish to return now to my reservation about the five year trial period. We have already had one five year trial period, much of which has been wasted because the government and the department ignored, neglected or deliberately decided to do little or nothing in the way of research that would have provided the basic data and hard facts about murder on which a better informed judgment could have been made of this question at this time. I realize that
26314-34J

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
Professor Fattah's study has been published, but its terms of reference were limited primarily to the deterrent effect of capital punishment. Professor Ciale of the University of Ottawa is engaged in a more in depth study, but when will it be available? At the committee stage, I would like to see an amendment introduced reducing the trial period from five to two years, during which intensive efforts would be made to correlate information about those who have committed murder with mental stability, social and economic background, motivations, and many other factors, for I am convinced that not only murder but most crime is rooted in our slums, in our broken homes, in our deprived areas and with our deprived citizens.
Capital punishment is not the answer to the eradication of crime, but a concerted attack on the ills of society could be the answer. I urge this intensive study, Mr. Speaker, for we know so little about the reasons that turn people into criminals. In this connection, I wish to recount an incident which took place recently in one of our federal institutions. Dr. Jean Vanier was speaking to a group of about 200 inmates and his message to them was his well known appeal for change, for sharing, for love. "Every man has the right to know he is loved," he concluded.
A moment of silence followed Dr. Vanier's address. Then, one inmate in the audience burst out in an emotional indictment of the social conditions which brought him to a long sentence in prison. His words were like these: "You were speaking about, like, children going through hell. Well, you had it easy. You don't know what it's like to have your bloody brother stand by when you're eight years old while boy friends rape you. You don't know what its like to be burned with a cigarette. "You don't know what it's like to be six years old, and your junky old man comes home too sick to think, and you reach out and you cook the dust for him. Friends call you from the lane. You go to the window and say 'Wait a minute.'
"Your little sister bumps you. Out goes the fist with the fix. Your old man jumps from where he is sitting at the table, kicks you in the head and breaks your jaw, picks you up and throws you clear across the room against the wall. "You don't know what its like to have to steal out of parked cars and sell in pawn shops to feed yourself and your little twin sister, your kid brother and kid sister. And you have to end up hustling your body when you're nine years old because you can't provide no more by stealing- you can't get enough to fill their needs.
"You don't know what it's like to end up trying to escape the same way your folks tried to escape, with a fix, and you're ten years old-having to hustle even more. "You don't know what it's like to be 11 years old and walk into the room at 2 o'clock in the morning just to have the man in blue grab you and haul you away to a reform school until they can find a foster home for you, because they have busted your folks, and you have to bounce around. "Until you know-until the world knows and does something about it they better never speak to me about love cause I'll kick their head in!" That was the answer given to Dr. Vanier.
Until we know-until we know that it is situations like this in which crime flourishes and escalates-until we are

willing to face up to the relationship between crime and social and economic injustice, we shall go on arguing and agonizing about the band-aid approach of capital punishment to a deeply ingrained cancerous illness which afflicts our nation.
Let us bring this debate to a quick conclusion so that we can direct our efforts and our energies to tackling the problem at its roots.
Some hon. Merfibers: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a debate centering on the government's proposal for suspension of the law on capital punishment in Canada for a further five year period. It is an important debate and is being followed, I am sure, by a great many Canadians in every part of the country, but it is a curious debate. It is curious because the government, as far as I have been able to ascertain, has given no indication that in the event of the defeat of its proposal in parliament it will respect that decision any more than it respected the decision of parliament taken about six years ago requiring the death penalty for the murderers of prison guards.
Mr. Speaker, aside altogether from whether we favour abolition or restoration of capital punishment, and I have heard extremely good arguments on both sides, as we have heard them today, I submit that the government's failure to respect the decision of parliament, of this House and this body of people representing the people of Canada in the matter of carrying out the decision taken six years ago regarding capital punishment has, in my view, led to a lessening of public belief in parliament and to an eroding respect for that part of our democratic fabric known as the law of the land. Mr. Speaker, I say this is a curious discussion with great towering speeches which, so far as we know, will have no real effect on whether the policy of Canada will or will not be that of capital punishment. As has been said by a notable speaker of many centuries ago about the speeches of one of his contemporaries, "His speeches are like palm trees-they soar high but bear no fruit."
This is the first point I should like to make; that the government should state clearly that it will now respect the decision of parliament in this matter as to the retention, suspension or abolition of capital punishment. Otherwise, our talk here will be empty and those who sent us here will know it. It is natural that there has been a good deal of emotion in the speeches we have heard so far. The death penalty is a matter about which we are apt to have feelings and beliefs and/or prejudices that have their roots perhaps far back in our ancestral past. These feelings naturally influence our views and utterances on this subj ect.
For example, I suppose that we all know of people who will listen to no arguments for the abolition of capital punishment. Their hearts, and therefore their minds, are already made up. Some of them, surprisingly to me, are religious people. They are among the foremost in demanding restoration of the death penalty, seemingly not so much for any hope that it may save human life by acting as a deterrent. Really, as I understand their letters and I think many hon. members will have recieved similar let-
May 22, 1973

ters, these people have feelings and desires for retribution and indeed vengeance in this situation.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, we have abolitionists, not a few of them in my own party who recoil, who shut their ears and close their eyes to any arguments that it may well be right for a community to take a life which has destroyed the lives and liberties of other individuals and which threatens to do so again or which acts as an example, if unchecked, to others with like murderous or violent designs. No such prejudice motivates me, Mr. Speaker. I approach this subject as pragmatically as I did 15 years ago when I first proposed to the then Conservative government that consideration should be given to a five-year suspension of capital punishment for a trial period.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, as you may recall, back in 1958 there was at least in my part of the country, British Columbia, and no doubt other parts, a great controversy over the question of capital punishment or no capital punishment. Indeed, it continues to this day. It appeared to me then, and again in 1968 after I was elected to this House, that we should have a five-year or at least a test period without capital punishment. This came into being about 1967 and it was taken, I thought, after a great deal of soul-searching and debate and was supported by some members, including myself, solely on the basis that it would indeed provide some gauge or test of whether capital punishment was necessary in this modern age. I certainly supported that vote for the five-year suspension and, like many others, I kept track of the results of that five-year period.
The question I asked myself then and which I ask myself today is: does the absence of the law of capital punishment in the form of the death penalty utilized by the community, result in the increase in capital punishment which takes the form of murder by individuals who decree death and who carry out the execution of another? If it does, if the absence of capital punishment results in the loss of human life and liberty, then surely we must still, at this stage of our social development, retain it. If it does not, if collective capital punishment is not a deterrent to individual capital punishment, then I believe we should get rid of it.
In making the representation for a five-year trial period suspension of the death penalty in Canada in 1968, I did so as a writer, not then a member of this House. My feeling then and since has been the pragmatic one that such a test period could help to provide the public, the parliament and government of our country with a gauge to help to decide whether people still require the preventive and deterrent factor of the death penalty. I did not know and I had on open mind. I retain that view.
As I have said, and as others have said, I kept close tabs on the result of the suspension of capital punishment. The result is disconcerting to those who claim that capital punishment does not deter killing. Statistics Canada has the record and the record is this. An average of 360 people, being about one per day, have been murdered per year in Canada during the five-year non-death penalty period as compared to 233 persons per year in the previous five-year period. In 1971, the last year for which I have records, the number of murders had risen to 422-this against the 233 figure when capital punishment was at least on the books.
Capital Punishment
That is an increase of 65 per cent in the number of murders during the five-year suspension period, from 1.3 murders per 100,000 population to 2.5 per cent. In light of those figures, I think the government would do well to take back the present proposal for a further five-year extension of the period of non-capital punishment.
Like the previous speaker, I would agree to a shorter period, say of two years. In view of the importance of the issue of violence, death, crime, and all the factors that are involved in it, I think the entire subject might be given further consideration and a more realistic decision might be arrived at than the one we are liable to arrive at now on the one or other side of this question. Certainly, the absence of capital punishment for murder in the past five year suspension period has been accompanied by a very substantial increase in the number of murders in Canada and the murder rate in Canada has gone up. The absence of the penalty, in my view, is not necessarily linked to the increase in the rate; nevertheless, it is there and I think that a further five year period of trial is too long. I think the further trial period should be for two years when, as I suggested, the whole matter could be further discussed.
It seems to me that those of us who wish and work for a more humane, more small "L" liberal, philosophy with respect to the rehabilitation of criminals should stop and take note of the fact that in recent years in North America it almost seems as if the rate of violent crime has been rising in direct proportion to the extension of so-called permissive steps. We will not help the improvement of the treatment of those who break the law if we close our eyes or our ears to the facts of life-in this case, to the facts of death. That will not help those who seek to reform our system of discipline. I think the reverse very likely will be the case.
In the light of the record of the previous five-year suspension of capital punishment period, in the light of the rising wave of crime and violence and the erosion of civil rights and liberty, I cannot support the present proposal of the government for a further five-year suspension of capital punishment. I think that if the suspension period were two years, as I have suggested, there might be a more comprehensive investigation of this cancer of violence which is afflicting North America in particular. I think a two-year ban would win support not only among members of this House, but among many members of the public who, having seen and felt the results of the first five-year suspension, would be unwilling to risk a second such period.
In conclusion, may I refer briefly to an article I wrote for the Toronto Star in the fall of 1971 on this subject. I said that the rate of murder in the suspension period up to that time was up by 53 per cent. Assaults were up by 52 per cent, according to my article. The rate for attempted murder had doubled in the same period, and so on. In fairness, I also noted that in 1970 one fire accounted for 40 victims, but only one person was charged. That should not be overlooked. Nevertheless, the rate of violent crimes had increased and has increased since then in Canada. These factors are important in determining how we are to review the matter of parole, sentencing, and rehabilitation procedures, which we are trying to improve.

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
We are dealing with a subject of extreme and vital importance to all Canadians, and I think we had better deal with it before, as has happened in many American cities, it is unsafe for us to walk alone at night and citizens, knowing themselves to be without real protection from violence by their constituted authorities, take the law into their own hands in the form of guns. If that happens, we will have everybody's law, which is nobody's law, and murders and violent crimes will grow among us. I, for one, hope to see us taking logical and sensible action on the issue before us. In my opinion, it is preferable that we not have a five-year suspension of capital punishment but a two-year suspension period. If that were done, we might well offset something, which I foresee arising in addition to crimes of violence, namely, an outraged and fearful public, whose backlash can erode our civil liberties just as surely as those are now threatened by the violent.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some members regard this debate on capital punishment as a waste of time because each member knows how he or she will vote, irrespective of the speeches of colleagues. However, I think the debate has been good, because it has shown the serious division of opinion not only in this House, but among the public. Thus there is no immediate answer that will receive genuine, widespread approval. We must search for the best possible solution that will ensure as much as possible the proper penalty for murder and the security of the state.
As we know, and as those who have taken part in the debate have dwelt on, we have been asked to debate a bill that has three purposes: To reinstate the five-year extension of the ban on hanging, which expired on December 29, 1972, and to extend the ban to December 31, 1977; to eliminate the term "capital murder" in relation to murder punishable by life imprisonment; and to ensure that the definition of murder punishable by death refers to the murder of a police officer and prison guard, and so on.
The main issue, as we know, is whether Canada should abolish or retain capital punishment. Since 1962, no one has been hanged in Canada, and although there have been four convictions for the murders of police officers since 1968, the cabinet has commuted each one. Studies about the effects of capital punishment as a deterrent are inconclusive, not only in Canada but in other countries. For instance, the New Zealand experience of abolition and reinstatement of capital punishment shows that there is no significant effect on the murder rate.
From this point I want to develop my argument in depth Mr. Speaker, so I wonder if I could call it five o'clock and return to my remarks after the supper recess.

CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
that Bill C-17, to amend the Canada Elections Act (permanent voters' list), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-17, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act, is to change our present system of enumeration and to provide a permanent voters list. I am proposing this bill with the full understanding of the objections raised by such people as the Chief Electoral Officer and the representation commissioner about the feasibility of such a system. Our present system may be good; however, the problems of disenfranchisement, particularly those of the last election, indicate to many of us that it is not good enough. We, as a nation possessing high quality technical and human resources are capable of something better.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I should like to briefly outline why a change is needed in our present system, why a permanent voters' list would be more advantageous and what some of the possible systems are that we might borrow from or adopt. It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, that all members of this House are concerned that thousands of Canadians are denied the right to participate on the most fundamental level of our political system, elections. It is my hope that out of a concern for this problem, the members of this House will refer Bill C-17 to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that a thorough and extensive discussion of this important question can take place.
As in many western democracies, the concept of political participation plays a very important role within the Canadian political system. The right of a Canadian citizen to vote in elections has evolved from a period of restricted male suffrage to our almost complete state of universal suffrage. Because we have not always enjoyed universal suffrage, Canadians regard highly their right, at one time
May 22, 1973

their privilege, to participate in the electoral process. Compared to our neighbour to the south, we enjoy a relatively high enumerated voter turnout with some 70 to 80 per cent voting at each federal election. Thus, when the right to participate is denied a legitimate claimant, there is a grave and serious problem that must be overcome. The individual voter is upset and so are the foundations of our democratic system.
Our experience, particularly that of the last election, tells us that a great number of eligible Canadian voters were not enumerated and were unable to vote. During the election campaign of 1972, newspaper editorials and letters to the editor pointed daily to the inadequacies of our present system of enumeration. Many blamed these inadequacies on the new electoral law, on the shortage of time in which the election was called or on the fact that there were not enough good people to carry out the enumeration properly. However, problems such as these have existed in the past and we have coped with them. However, with the increasing population and the growing complexity and mobility of Canadian society, their present adequacy is in question.
Failure on the part of our present system to enumerate those who have a permanent and fixed residence is only one problem. It has been estimated that at least 6 per cent of these potential voters are not enumerated. There is another larger group of citizens who are continually disenfranchised because our present system has an enormous difficulty in coping with their residence status at the time of an election. These are the eligible voters who are living away from home, within or outside Canada, at the time of the election or those who are travelling here or abroad. The Canada Elections Act of 1970 did make provisions for proxy voting for fishermen, prospectors, the physically ill and students. However, the procedure involved is almost intimidating to the potential voter. For those Canadians who are travelling or temporarily living abroad, no real provision for absentee voting exists. At present, before this House, there are three bills, C-43, C-56, and C-140, and one motion that are attempting to rectify this problem and extend the franchise to those who are excluded. It is my belief that a permanent electoral list would provide the necessary checks and information to facilitate absentee and proxy balloting.
Poor enumeration can restrict people from voting but, perhaps more important, it can foster feelings of alienation and/or discontent among those affected. Even if people want to vote, they seem reluctant to overcome the obstacle of not having been enumerated. Often they turn to one of their candidates for help, but in a great many cases they are too late and succeed only in further aggravating themselves.
Another problem that supports the argument for a change in the system is the length of our present campaign and the resulting time span between parliaments. In the 1970's, with our systems of transportation and communication, one wonders if a 60-day election campaign is not an anachronism. Long campaigns involve an excessive wastage of time, energy and money. The public become saturated to the point of distinterest by the continual bombardment of events and news of the election. A shorter
Canada Elections Act
election campaign would ease the physical and emotional burden of all those concerned, including the candidates.
Of greater importance is the fact that the inevitable disruption in government caused by elections could become a serious problem. Since 1867, the average time between the date of the election and the first day of the new parliament is 82.7 days. On 20 occasions since 1867, the period has been more than 60 days. If we add this period to a long election campaign, almost a third of our year has vanished. In the world today, things happen too fast. If emergencies arise or problems have to be dealt with, will our present system allow us to adequately deal with them?
In trying to evaluate and compare systems of enumeration, I think that there are four basic criteria which should be kept in mind; first, comprehensiveness of enumeration; second, possible effects on voter turnout; third, time required to hold the election after the election writ is issued and, fourth, cost per person enumerated. It seems highly possible that we can develop a system of a permanent electoral list, which is updated periodically and which may be revised up to the fifteenth day before polling day, which would surpass our present system on all of the basic criteria except the fourth, cost per person enumerated. I would like to discuss briefly some of the present systems of permanent voter lists in our country and elsewhere, and to point out their advantage in the areas of enumeration, voter turnout and time. Before proceeding with this, I think it is necessary to examine the question of cost.
Nelson Castonguay in his report on "Methods of Registration of Elections and Absentee Voting" in 1968 concluded, and I quote:
The system of continuous electoral rolls currently in use in the Commonwealth of Australia, including the method of compulsory registration on the part of the electors, can be adapted for use in federal elections in Canada, to reduce the time required for the holding of elections and to provide improved facilities for voting by electors.
However, he felt that such a system would be very costly. Other analysts have reached the same conclusion, that a permanent electoral list would cost more. The important question must then be asked: Are the benefits that will be derived from a permanent list worth the cost? If a permanent voters' list means that fewer people will be left off the rolls, the answer must be yes. In addition, if the same list were utilized by other levels of government, the provinces and municipalities, the cost per voter at each election would be significantly reduced.
On a more practical level, it must be noted that we have experienced an election every 3.6 years since confederation. When elections have been close together, such as the ones in 1957 and 1958, the cost of the latter enumeration has been very low. In 1957, 4.38 persons were enumerated per dollar spent. In the present period, when parliaments do not sit the full five years, the cost of the permanent list will not be as great as predicted.
Another practical administrative detail that should be considered is the problem of getting a sufficient number of relatively competent enumerators in the future. This problem was used as an excuse during the last election. Effective implementation of a permanent list, which would be

May 22, 1973
Canada Elections Act
updated annually and have provisions for revision prior to the election, would require a permanent staff, and temporary employees needed could be used every year. If Canada were to adopt a system with a permanent electoral list, we would have to tailor one to meet our own needs. Because of our geographic size and the mobility of our population, it is clear that a permanent list, if it is to be an effective one, must not only be updated periodically, but must also be subject to revision quite close to election day.
The province of British Columbia and the Commonwealth of Australia are two examples of systems of continuous electoral rolls allowing revision up to a fixed date before polling day. From the Representation Commissioner's report of 1968 on "Methods of Registration of Electors and Absentee Voting", I should like to summarize the main points of these two systems and the benefits afforded by others mentioned.
In British Columbia, no yearly registration campaign takes place. Persons duly registered who vote at each election have their names retained on the electoral rolls. If a person moves and notifies the Registrar of the fact, the rolls are amended accordingly. If he does not so notify the Registrar, he may vote by absentee ballot as if residing at his former address, provided such address can be considered his place of residence by the terms of the Elections Act. Registrars keep their rolls up to date throughout the year by the addition of new registrations and by noting changes of address forwarded to them by the electors concerned. Registered persons who did not vote in the election are sent postcards and if they are returned undelivered, their name is taken off the rolls. Several years ago, all the rolls were cancelled and a complete registration took place. The method usually employed to keep the rolls uo to date is to cancel the rolls for certain electoral districts and take a door-to-door canvass, carried out by enumerators to compile new rolls for those districts. In other electoral districts, a partial cancellation may take place with registration centres set up at convenient places for the use of electors. Before the 1966 election, all registered voters were sent a card telling them they were eligible to vote. Those cards which were returned indicated to the registrar that the voter had changed his status in some way. A massive advertizing campaign encouraged those who did not receive cards to register at local centres or by mail. The onus to register is thus placed on the individual. The mailing procedure is supplemented periodically by a door-to-door campaign. Since there is a permanent list, a relatively secure system of absentee voting is possible.
Under the Australian system, enrolment as an elector is compulsory and responsibility for enrolment rests on the elector. In order to be enrolled, persons must sign an electoral claim which is available from all post offices and electoral offices. An annual review of the urban areas is carried out by casual labour making use of such aids as death certificates, prison records, etc. In rural areas, this review is undertaken by means of an electoral agency system which employes persons, usually public officers such as postmasters and police officers, who are appointed to note the changes which have taken place. Postal voting is permitted in Australia for several classes of citizens

who may be absent from their electoral division on polling day. This privilige extends to citizens travelling under conditions that may preclude voting-including travelling abroad-or who are seriously ill, infirm, or, in the case of women, approaching maternity, or members of certain religious orders. The percentage of electors voting by post generally averages from 2 to 3 per cent of the total vote polled.
As in the case of other methods of voter registration, it is difficult to judge with accuracy the success of the enumeration undertaken. Under these systems, a great deal of emphasis is placed on the elector, the on-going updating that takes place, and the revision before an election. Under these systems voter registration is facilitated and encouraged, and late revision allows any concerned individual the opportunity to vote. When permanent lists are established, many persons who are normally excluded by other systems are able to vote by absentee or postal ballot. Moreover, the time needed before an election can be greatly reduced. In Great Britain, three weeks is all that is needed because no provision is made for revision. In Canada, the period of time needed would be four to five weeks.
The problems of complete enumeration will probably forever plague us. If we entrust the citizens of our country with the duty or responsibility of registration, then only they are to blame for any shortcomings. If this duty or responsibility is further strengthened by legislation and a systematic review, a great deal will have been done to encourage maximum participation at the electoral level.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, we can do better than our present system. To my mind, a permanent electoral list affords the best opportunity to bring about meaningful and necessary changes. As active participants in the last election, we are aware of the problem involved. There is a real need to review our present system and perhaps make a change-if only temporary in nature. It is my hope that Bill C-17, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act, will get second reading today and be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections so that we, as Members of Parliament, can discuss, and make recommendations on, this most important question.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. gentleman who has just spoken for his very fine research as well as for his sense of priorities. I think it is important we should constantly take stock of our electoral machinery and seek means whereby we can improve the process of elections.
After a good many years of studying many jurisdictions,
I believe we are much blessed in this country; we have a very fine election doctrine and a good elections Act. A good election process is, it seems to me, far more important than a grandiose Bill of Rights-some countries have the latter in abundance but on polling day the practice and the theory are often far removed. We are intent on improving the Elections Act.
I believe every member will agree with me that we have been fortunate during many years that the person occupying the office of Chief Electoral Officer has been a man of ability and impartiality. We are blessed in this. I agree
May 22, 1973

with the hon. member that there are always areas in which improvement is possible. It used to be the practice that as soon as was reasonably possible after an election, the whole of the Elections Act was sent to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for careful examination. Whenever this was done, good suggestions were forthcoming. We did learn lessons during the last election. We found that mistakes had been made, and the day will come when these will need to be considered. For example, there were too many spoiled ballots. I have been a member of the committee for almost ten years-I am almost like a Father of Confederation on that committee. We thought what was done would be an improvement, but, somehow, we erred. Perhaps the city of Ottawa has come up with a better ballot, one with a circle. This is a matter which will have to be considered.
There is, of course, no perfect solution, no way of attaining that glorious day when every single qualified elector will find his name on the list. I agree with the hon. member that it is far better to be working on the list, structuring the list, at a time other than the beginning of a campaign. We found during the last election that it was a mad scramble to get information about the enumerators available to the returning officers 59 days ahead rather than 54. Even in a highly-organized, progressive and perceptive constituency like Hillsborough, where people have shown their good judgment for a long time, some effort was required to get those names in. So, people are appointed quickly, they do not have time in which to receive the necessary instruction, and they have to carry out their duties quickly.
It would be far better, in my judgment, as in the judgment of the hon. member, if there were an office, an emanation of the state, in which the lists were brought up to date regularly. I like the hon. member's suggestion that other jurisdictions could use the list. If they were smart enough, they could do so. But we need to be sensible about this; we cannot have one province saying a person is mature enough to vote at 19 while others say they are not mature until they reach the age of 21. Some pattern of co-operative federalism needs to be forthcoming. I should like to see an officer appointed who would look after the registration of voters. Other jurisdictions would make use of that office. The hon. member suggested that lists be kept open closer to the election date. Some countries open the lists only once a year, which allows for too much slipping in the accuracy of the list. He thought the list should be open until 15 days before polling. In other words, you would get 99.9 per cent of the job done. Then, you have properly trained officials with the required expertise who do their very best to get the other names in.
I quite agree with the hon. member that, while it is easy to say that if a citizen wants to vote he should make sure his name is on the list, we have found that that is not enough. This is the point of having revising officers and agents under the act. All of those involved in party politics-some of us get involved in that at election time, if not at any other time-would suggest we could give a little nudge there so people will get their names on the list. Parties spend money on advertising and I think they could suggest to these people that they put their names on the
Canada Elections Act
list. I am sure that every member of this House has been with the person whose name, by jove, is not on the list, but they do not tell you until it is too late, which is a most unfortunate thing. All people should be able to exercise this important act of citizenship, namely the right to vote.
I am not going to predict that we are going to have a series of minority governments; I think we will sweep through and have a comfortable majority next time. But the question is all the more serious if we are going to have elections every two and a half or two and a third years. I have gone through seven elections now. Constitutionally, we say it is a five year term, but politically it is a four year term. I should be 100 instead of looking like 100. If we are going to have the disruption of dissolution-and that does disrupt the country-there is also disruption in having a series of minority governments, so let us try and get some permanency into our structure by making provision for a permanent voters list.
Another argument that the hon. member put forth in a very reasoned and well organized presentation, if I may say so, was that his proposal would allow for absentee voting. I have always found that proxy voting is not enough, though there were certain examples in the last election that showed that proxy voting was too much. However, that was an aberration of the system, certainly not the purpose for which it was intended. The absentee voting system can function well, and in a practical way, if we have a permanent voters' list. We live in a more mobile society than ever before, and there are Canadians all across the country and in many parts of the world whose interest in, knowledge of and concern for, the parliamentary process is not vitiated by the distance they happen to be from their home. We can hardly expect Canadians to sit around waiting in case someone calls an election, and one of the great uncertainties of our system is that we are never quite sure when an election will be called.
I have also heard, as has the hon. member, of this question of expense, but I am not so frightened of that. I suppose having spent so many years in this place I have watched the big money spenders in action time and time again. However, I believe that once established, in view of the increasing cost of enumeration as election follows election, the cost differential will not be so enormous. Even if it would be more costly, the question we ask is not that but: Will it allow more Canadians to exercise their franchise? On that test, and on that test only, in my opinion, should this proposed bill be viewed. After the most careful consideration of the matter, I believe we would be well advised to push this bill on to committee, and in committee I do not think I would have the slightest hesitation in supporting it and doing everything possible to have it become part of our election structure before we next go to the polls.
I close, as I began, by commending the hon. member and assuring him of my complete support for his efforts to improve our election machinery.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill presented by the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan), I want to say at the outset that I agree with his motives, which I think are to make it possible for the largest number of Canadians to be in a position to exercise their franchise. I think this is the hon.

May 22, 1973
Canada Elections Act
member's main motive. His second motive is to shorten the election campaign period, and I want to take some issue with that. However, I am glad that he has brought this bill forward. I have no objection to its passing second reading and going to the committee on Privileges and Elections because it is unlikely that we will be dealing with electoral law of much more significance than this, namely the matter of the control and limitation of election expenses.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), myself and several other hon. members were members of the committee on privileges and elections in 1968 and 1969 when the committee dealt with the report of the commissioner, Mr. Castonguay, on a permanent voters list. If I am not incorrect, I believe the committee was unanimous in accepting Mr. Castonguay's report. Although the cost of the hon. member's proposal would be two to four times as high as the cost of the present system of enumeration, given a country with our kind of geography, mobility of population-a matter the hon. member for London West mentioned in presenting his bill-climate, living habits and a number of other factors, we chose to accept the report of the electoral commissioner.
This is not to say that the principle of a permanent list is invalid. Perhaps over the next number of months or years parliamentarians and people expert in electoral law may come up with a system that suits our needs. But let us not be under any illusion as to what will be the cost. In 1967 and 1968 when the electoral commission was conducting their investigations, they estimated the cost at $1 per voter. We suspect that by now the cost would be $1.50 per voter. If one updated the list once a year, that would entail spending $20 million to $30 million a year on maintaining a reasonably accurate and updated permanent voters list.
However, even a permanent list will always be out of date to some extent. We should remind ourselves that there are literally tens of thousands of people in this country who choose not to vote for religious, political or economic reasons, or a combination of all three. I would not be surprised if they amounted to one or two per cent of the electorate. They are people who will not vote for a variety of reasons, no matter how accurate the method of putting their names on the list.
I must also comment on the fact that in the course of the meetings of the committee on privileges and elections we talked with people from other countries, and I was surprised to find how complimentary they were about our method of enumeration, bad though we think it is. I have listened to people from Puerto Rico, Australia and some of the states of the United States being very complimentary to us in terms of the method we use in trying to enumerate the maximum number of people possible prior to a general election. So let us look both at what we are now doing to improve the system and at the establishment of a permanent list, something I do not foresee happening until at least one or two further general elections have been called. In light of the present parliamentary set-up, it is unlikely that a permanent list could be established.
However, we could make some relatively simple amendments to the present electoral law to increase the eligibility of the number of people able to vote on election day. Some of these have already been mentioned such as, for

example, a method for absentee balloting and a larger number of days for advance polls.
We have had reference, also, to swearing in at rural polls as well as urban polls. I had the misfortune of driving three different voters to the polls on election day in Regina last fall, all of whom thought they were on the enumerator's list because they had that little slip of paper which the enumerator had left with them. They did not read the slip of paper carefully enough and thought their names were on the list. They were all born and raised in this country, but could not vote. Had they lived a mile, or even one yard, outside the city limits of Regina they could have cast a ballot in a rural poll by being sworn in. This situation seems to me to be intrinsically unfair. These are some of the things we could do now to improve the present system.
I wish to take some issue with the remarks of the hon. member about shortening the election period. His riding is London West. I do not know how much rural area he has in his riding. It is all very well for members who can walk around the constituency in a day because it is a mile wide and three miles long to talk about shortening the election period, but they should think of their colleagues who have 40, 60 or 80 communities in their constituencies. These members, even if they spent half a day in each community, would not be able to cover all of them between the time the election is called and the time the vote is cast. Members such as the hon. member for London West should think about other members who are entitled to as much opportunity as anyone else to visit a maximum number of their constituents. This is what I meant when I spoke about taking our geography into account when talking about the election period which it is alleged we could shorten by having a permanent voters' list.
My riding is of moderate size. It encompasses nearly
6,000	square miles. In it there are between 40 and 50 hamlets, villages and towns, in addition to half the city of Regina. I am ashamed to say that there were 12 or 14 locations which I did not have time to visit during the last election campaign. My campaign manager tells me, however, that this might have been a good thing, because I won in two or three of them. If one were to follow that argument to its logical conclusion, we would all stay home for the entire campaign and still be re-elected.
When talking about a permanent list, I believe it is legitimate to remember our geography and our climate, as well as how difficult it is for candidates of all parties in a reasonable manner and in a meaningful way to visit a maximum number of their constituents. If the election period were shortened in terms of the period between the time the writs are issued and election day, it would mean that the voters in a number of constituencies of Canada would have much less opportunity to see, meet, hear and question their candidates.
I feel, and have felt for some time-and this provision was included in the government's proposed bill last year on the control and limitation of election expenses-that the public is angry about the high cost of election campaigns and the continual bombardment on radio, television and the press for seven or eight weeks by all the
May 22, 1973

political parties and their candidates. The bill which the government brought forward last year proposed to limit the period in which that kind of campaign could take place to the last 28 days of the campaign. I submit that that is the kind of shortening of the campaign period the people of Canada want.
Most of the people are not particularly interested in, and do not care about the mechanics of setting up the election machinery, and so on. However, all of us who are experienced in respect of returning officers, election clerks, the Chief Electoral Officer and his staff, as well as the amount of work they have to do even once the election machinery is all set up, know that there is need for every possible day because of our thinly spread population, our geography and the problem of communications. So I submit we should look into this question and do everything we can to devise a permanent voters' list. In the meantime, there are a number of things which could be done to make the electoral process much better than it is now, by using the present law.
Proposals for a permanent voters' list have taken a number of different forms. From what I have been able to find out from the people who lived in British Columbia in the first few years when they had a so-called permanent list, it would seem that it was a debacle, a complete disaster, in some parts of the province. A large percentage of the population was unable to vote on election day. I have heard complaints about this type of system from people in Australia and Puerto Rico. However, that is their problem.
One could think of placing in a computer the name of every person in Canada and running the names off according to their social insurance numbers. In that way we might have a permanent list. The date of birth of each person would have to be on the social insurance card. The information on the social insurance card, which everybody has, ought to be sufficient. The card could be presented at the polling booth with other appropriate identification. Perhaps that would accomplish the purpose, or perhaps the Canadian citizenship card would accomplish the purpose.
The question is whether every voter would carry his card to the poll on election day. We all know the answer to that question. There would be those who would say that they had left the card in their other suit, or that it has been lost or stolen. Also, there would be the possibility of fraud. But I submit that no matter what kind of electoral system we have, there always will be the possibility of fraud. However, since such a tiny percentage of the electorate would resort to fraud, I would rather err on the side of making it as easy as possible for people to vote while maintaining reasonable safeguards.
This is a good bill for us to discuss and to turn over to the committee. I find it passing strange-or perhaps it is not too strange-that there is silence again by members of the government and of the official opposition concerning legislation on the control and limitation of election expenses. Unless we have some measure of control in this respect, a permanent list, enumeration or whatever method is used, the system will still involve wholesale inequities and there will still be in the minds of Canadi-
Canada Elections Act
ans suspicion about how our elections are financed. I submit that much of the suspicion is justified.
In view of the scandals in our history, and the use to which political contributions have been put recently in the United States, it is all the more urgent that strong, effective and forcible legislation be brought in at once. Since 1966 I have listened ad nauseam to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He said this reform is a must, a high priority item. I listened last year to the members of the government when they brought in a bill with two major loopholes in it which rendered meaningless the entire legislation. There was a limitation on candidates, but no limitation on parties. Isn't that handy for the bagmen of the old-line parties? There was not even an attempt at a modest form of disclosure, which rendered meaningless everything else in that bill.
I hope the House will agree to send this bill to the committee and that the government very shortly, I hope tomorrow, will bring in a half decent bill to control and limit election expenses.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to speak in favour of Bill C-17, in the interest of greater democratization, so that democracy will apply to all citizens, without restriction or bias, because it is well-known that when an election is announced, a voters list is hastily put together, made up of members of political parties who are committed people, not necessarily objective, and that during election campaigns you often come across passions and hatred in constituencies, with the result that the enumerators are often somewhat less than objective.
This is how certain abuses have been discovered in the past. Voters from areas that supported an opposition candidate were simply not on the voters list. This even happened in my constituency, during the last elections. Most of the tenants in the same block of apartments who shared the same political opinions were not to be found on the voters list. This is something that would not happen if we had a permanent voters list. These deliberate omissions could not occur, since people would have enough time to correct them.
Some elderly citizens, for example, who had lived in the same place within the same municipality for maybe 50 years, ever since they were born, discovered upon arriving at the polling station that their names were not on the list, that they had no more privileges than if they were Africans or Europeans. This sort of thing could not happen if we had a permanent voters list.
I will not comment on what is done in a move under hand manner, "fiddling" with lists, etc. In addition, the names of some individuals appearing on lists shown in public places, on posts for example, may not be included in the official book. When the official voters list will be used on voting day, these people will be unable to vote.
At the present time, there is no previous registration in rural areas, that is people vote if they can prove that they live in the area. There is no problem in that connection. Thus, the permanent voters list could perhaps apply only to urban areas, since this is were problems are found. A permanent list could be drawn up in cities. Such a system

May 22, 1973
Canada Elections Act
has been established in Quebec this year. This very month, enumerators have undertaken their work even if no election has been called.
There would be no objection for the federal government nor the Quebec government to use the Quebec permanent electoral list, since in that province as in the federal system the same voting rules apply, I mean all citizens over 18 have the right to vote. The federal government could use those lists and pay a financial compensation to the province of Quebec for saving it the trouble of doing that work.
In those cases where there are provincial electoral lists, the federal government could use them without having to incur additional expenses to establish its own.
Speaking of costs, I do not think it is a sound argument, at a time when we genuinely want to democratize politics, when we really want to give all citizens the opportunity to express themselves, to defeat a government, as will happen, I hope, at the next elections. I think such thing is priceless. I much prefer paying a few cents more to give the franchise to a 50-year old who has always lived where he is to vote than to see others pass "telegraphs".
At this time, every one in Canada has a social insurance number. Now I suggest that the electoral officer might consider using that number to draw up the permanent list. No extraordinary expense would be involved and even if 10, 20 or 100 citizens bear the same name identification would be achieved through the different numbers.
I shall not go further into this issue as I should like to see this bill put in order that it may be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.
