subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments for which I spoke before the dinner recess I stated that in this critical debate we must search for the best solution possible that will ensure justice, the proper penalty for murder and the security of society. We are dealing here with the highest question Members of Parliament can face, the question of life itself. We cannot slough off our responsibilities in the guise of adhering to questionable public opinion surveys. We are responsible to our constituents and to parliament itself to use our best judgment in resolving the capital punishment issue. The people who sent us here must be able to evaluate our reasoning process.
My mail on this issue has been sharply split into the retentionist and abolitionist camps. I will quote two letters, expressing opposite opinions, which are reflective of the opinions expressed in my mail. Mr. Robert B. Manly, of Edmonton, writes:
My family, my friends and neighbours with whom we have discussed the matter are deeply concerned with the increasing lawlessness in Canada, especially the increase in the number of murders and other crimes of violence. We are therefore strongly opposed to any extension of the present ban on the death penalty .... No one is afraid to commit murder any longer in Canada. Even when, despite all the technicalities which hamper police officers in obtaining evidence and getting convictions, a conviction is obtained, our judges and juries have been too lenient, judges frequently giving out sentences that are absurdly inadequate.
The only real deterrent to vicious crime is the certainty, upon conviction, of adequate punishment. In the case of premeditated murder such punishment must be the death penalty. Even the most vicious murderers do fear the death penalty. They certainly don't fear a sentence of four years in prison.
An opposite view is expressed by Mr. and Mrs. Lavern Burkhardt who urged me as in follows in a telegram:
Please support legislation to entirely abolish capital punishment irrespective of type of victim. We favour life imprisonment for a minimum period of 25 years. Executing convicted murderers sparks more sympathy for executed person than for victim. Death is not a greater deterrent than imprisonment. Civilized people should not be vindictive.
The weight of my mail is on the Manly, retentionist, side rather than the Burkhardt, abolitionist, side. But as I studied the opinions expressed to me I became convinced that most of those who support the death penalty do so out

May 22, 1973

of a desire for more safety in society and less so for revenge or retributive justice. In the present mood of Canada it is not enough simply to be an abolitionist or a retentionist. The people are clearly disturbed at the rising crime rate and want more protection. More than a "yes" or "no" on the question of capital punishment is called for.
Another constituent, Hans D. Ehrenlechner wrote me. It was his letter which most clearly pointed out a moderate course for the country to follow. Here is what Mr. Ehrenlechner wrote:
As a voting member in your constituency, I would like to express by deep concern over the forthcoming decision by free vote to either completely abolish or reinstate the practice of capital punishment in some form.
From a religious, metaphysical and moral point of view I am most certainly opposed to the reinstatement of capital punishment in any form whatsoever. However, we live in an imperfect world and such a step would likely not accomplish in practice what theoretically it should-i.e., contribute to the humanization of our society. Nor do I feel that the majority of citizens want and expect total abolition of the death penalty. You must be aware of the rising concern over lawlessness which the average voter believes is taking a sharp upward trend in recent years, and all those who advocate the reinstitution of the death penalty rest their case on this and similar grounds.
Mr. Ehrenlechner continues:
Surely there is an alternative solution to the problem that would both serve to protect the public-which should be the first concern of the law-and yet not detract from the high standards and ideals it is in our power to realize in this generation.
Having thought about the matter for some time, I feel that the only fair course of action at this time is to initiate another five-year extension on the banning of capital punishment in Canada. Reluctantly, I agree that the capital punishment be retained for the murder of policemen, prison guards, etc., and all those whose lives would be immediately endangered by the absence of any form of capital punishment. Again, from an aesthetic point of view this discrimination between police officers and the general public does not make sense, but then we are dealing with an emotional issue here and any strictly intellectual or "religious" arguments could hardly come up with a solution acceptable to the people.
Mr. Ehrenlechner closes his arguments this way:
One further point. Let's put a stop to the farce of life imprisonment. If we are to relax the laws in some respects, let's at least enforce the ones we have. I'm sure you've heard the stories about the Parole Board and their candied sugar-plum attitude to criminals, lax granting of paroles and easy bail for law breakers. Our entire judicial system, and the government backing it, is to be severely reprimanded in this respect.
I am of the opinion also that an enforced sentence of life imprisonment would equal or even excel capital punishment as an effective deterrent to crime, if an effective deterrent exists, that is.
I have gone into some detail in revealing the various views of my constituents to indicate that I have taken them most seriously into consideration. It was through this correspondence that I realized just how strong is the desire for improved security in our country today. We are paying a heavy price for the permissiveness of modern society. But I have to ask myself if the death penalty will achieve the safety the people want. Thus, I have examined that precise question.
There is no way that I can abdicate my responsibility to use my conscience in forming my decision as to how to vote. Some people think a Member of Parliament is a
Capital Punishment
delegate to carry out automatically the wishes of the majority of his constituents, assuming the majority can be defined. But that is not my concept of the job. I believe a person is elected by constituents who repose a sense of confidence, for the time being at least, in his judgment and expect him to use it. The assurance that he will always vote according to his conscience is the best service that a Member of Parliament can offer his constituents.
The starting point for my analysis of the capital punishment issue is my belief in the sanctity of life. When a murderer violates the sanctity of life by an act of violence on his victim, how is the sanctity of life preserved by another act of violence on the murderer, this time by the state? We are allowed to kill in self-defence, as we know, but for the state to execute a criminal is to perpetuate violence. I believe in a morality which excludes violence as permissible conduct. If we accepted execution as Retributive justice in an earlier period, we should be thankful that society is becoming more sensitive and that there is a movement throughout the world for total abolition. I agree with the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) who said when introducing the present bill in the House:
The state must set the clear example of respect for human life, through the tolerant and patient application of law which looks to other more effective means of protecting society and discouraging crime, even murder.
In addition to the philosophical side of this question one must study the practical. As many have noted, the strongest argument for retention is that capital punishment acts as a deterrent. But does it? The government sponsored the now famous study of the deterrent effect of capital punishment by Dr. Ezzar A. Fattah, associate professor of criminology at the University of Montreal. Dr. Fattah studied the circumstances surrounding the slight increase in criminal homicide in Canada over the past eight years and concluded that the increase could not be attributed to the suspension of capital punishment. The increase in criminal homicide is the lowest among all crimes of violence studied, a fact, he says, which indicates that such increase can neither be attributed nor related to the suspension of capital punishment. In short, Dr. Fattah concludes:
A study of homicide statistics in Canada jointly with the statistics of other crimes of violence and comparisons between the provinces and between the years do not lend support to the assumption of the uniquely deterrent effect of the death penalty. Thus, in deciding on the question of the reintroduction or abolition of capital punishment, reintroduction cannot be justified on the argument that it is a more effective deterrent to potential killers than the alternative of protected imprisonment.
Others in this debate have quoted statistics showing there does not seem to be any relationship between the existence of the death penalty and the rate of murder either in jurisdictions where capital punishment has given way to abolition, as in New Zealand, or contiguous abolitionist capital punishment states in the U.S.A. The case for deterrence has not been proved, and thus we cannot look to capital punishment for safety in society. On moral and practical grounds, then, full-scale capital punishment should not be reintroduced in Canada. And yet, as I have said, a simple abolitionist position is not sufficient.
The government has undermined the safety of society by giving the impression that all sentences of execution for killing policemen and jail guards are being automati-

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
cally commuted. We know that there have been no executions since 1962. Moreover, the escape rate of convicts, including killers, has been inordinately high, and the rehabilitative system of early parole and weekend passes scandalously lax. I believe the news coverage of the aberrations in the penal process has obscured much valuable rehabilitative work. None the less, as a result of government mismanagement the people feel that the rehabilitation of the prisoner has been given a higher priority than the protection of the public. The people need to be assured that public safety will be given a higher priority than prisoner rehabilitation.
I am convinced that minimum mandatory sentences for killing, and stricter enforcement in penitentiaries, will actually act as more of a deterrent and give the public a greater sense of security than capital punishment, which will likely be commuted and followed by parole only ten years after the crime. The question is: What is a minimum mandatory sentence? At first I thought the judge should make this determination in sentencing, but as a result of the impressions made on me by correspondents I now believe that parliament should fix the specific minimum sentence for premeditated murder at 25 years. Again, I say that such a well-publicized sentence will, in my opinion, act as a stronger deterrent than capital punishment which is rarely invoked.
Thus, I shall vote for Bill C-2 on second reading, because at the very least it extends the trial period of partial abolition for another five years. But the principal purpose of my affirmative vote is to send the bill to committee where the 25-year amendment can be examined. It may be that the committee, and ultimately parliament will decide that we do not yet have enough evidence to justify taking a definitive step. If so, the next step should be the appointment of a royal commission charged with responsibility for collecting the needed factual information and for conducting public hearings where individuals and groups can express their views.
There should be no hurry to come to a quick decision; it is better to take a slow course to help develop public understanding of the complexities of this issue. One of the benefits of such an organized examination would be to throw a spotlight on the reasons for violence in our society and its effect on the murder rate. As the United Church of Canada recently put it:
Our entire society needs creative outlets for expression of frustration or anger. Violence has become a way of life that we accept and that we condone in our so-called entertainment, and in our general approach to life. The death penalty is only one more violent reaction to violent action.
In other words, the causes of violence, from frustration through rage and all the way to murder, need to be examined so that we can purge our society of violence. A vast canvas will appear before us, including such factors as alcohol, drugs, gambling, emotional disorders, sexual deviation, the effects of brutalization dramatized on television, and the availability of deadly weapons. By reducing those elements in life which promote or lead to anti-social behavior we will be taking a big step forward, not only in the safety of society but in enhancing the dignity of human beings and the right to life itself.

If Bill C-2 fails to pass second reading, Mr. Speaker, then we will have reverted to capital punishment. Many people think that the simple act of retention will improve society. But it will not, for unless we get a better understanding of crime and what leads to it, unless we pass stringent gun control laws, unless we make productive and valuable citizens out of men and women who would otherwise lead lives of crime, we will be deluding ourselves that progress is being made. We will improve society by attacking the reasons for violence.
The public must be adequately protected. The guilty must be punished, and proper systems of reform maintained. But to take simple recourse in retribution is to close our eyes to the sanctity of life and the complexities underlying crime in modern society.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a new member rising to join in the debate on capital punishment cannot help but recall the speech delivered by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) shortly after this session began. At that time the dean of this House advised new members that their first speech would be the most difficult they would be called upon to deliver. While this is not my initial opportunity of speaking in the chamber, it is my first encounter with a speech on such a complex matter that is to be decided by what is termed a free vote. Out of respect for the sage counsel of the right hon. gentleman, I am inclined to agree that this is indeed the most difficult speech. Moreover, I hope that future events will bear out his words, as I cannot contemplate facing a more difficult challenge than that presented to every member by the question of capital punishment.
Certainly, I have never had to make as difficult a decision and I do pot believe that any more years of experiencing the workings of parliament, or experiencing life itself would have made the issue any clearer, the burden lighter or the decision easier. Rather, Mr. Speaker, I have spent the same months of study and research, anguish and soulsearching that have accompanied every member of this chamber in his or her consideration of the question of capital punishment. As we all know, the companion of this issue is the question, as old as parliament itself, as to the basis on which a member should decide how to vote. I believe that this latter, over-all question must be resolved before a member can begin to consider the specific legislation on which he shall vote.
My purpose, then, in rising today, Mr. Speaker, is to place before you and my colleagues, and before those whom I am honoured to represent, both my decision and the reasons for that decision-the basis on which I shall vote. I would no more have constituents agree with me for the wrong reasons than I would have them disagree because I failed to explain my position.
It is to the credit of all party leaders in this House that we are being given what is termed a free vote on this legislation. As a new member, I am particularly grateful to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) whom I am proud to support as leader of my party. The granting of this free vote acknowledges that the decision which hon. members are called upon to make transcends usual partisan considerations and so very deeply involves our con-
May 22, 1973

cepts of justice, morality, the powers of the state and, indeed, the value of human life.
We are summoned to this chamber to represent the people who have elected us. For whatever period they decide, we have the responsibility to share their dreams about this country, to advance their hopes, to voice their opinions and to ensure that they are represented when the decisions are made which affect their lives. I believe that my foremost responsibility is to represent here those who have sent me. Further, I believe that I represent them best when I act, on the basis of both intellect and conscience, to do what I honestly think is best for them and for our society.
This approach to my responsibilities is not to indicate that the views and feelings of my constituents should be unknown or unheeded by me. Quite the opposite. I am particularly grateful to the many who have taken the time and trouble to express their opinions on capital punishment. Every letter and conversation has received deep consideration and played a significant part in my decision.
I have tried to approach the extremely difficult question of capital punishment with an open mind and have weighed, to the best of my ability, the many and valuable arguments on both sides. All of us know that there are some people in this land who are so convinced their viewpoint is right that the possibility does not exist of there being another side to the question. No such intellectual luxury is open to the Member of Parliament, who must give fair and full consideration to all viewpoints. There is a tremendous gap between the onlooker who need only hold an opinion and the member of this House who must make the public decision on behalf of his constituents.
Of course, throughout the whole process of heartrending consideration I sought anxiously that one argument, that extra statistic, that new bit of information which would suddenly decide the question for me. As we all realize, no such convincing argument is to be found which would give us greater insight or more wisdom than that allowed to mortals. Rather, we have all sought and received from various sources the inconclusive statistics, the different viewpoints and the reams of information. It is left to us as individuals to consider all these things, to interpret them as best we can and then to face the questions. As uncertain as I am about this question and the ability of any man to deal with it, I do not shrink from the responsibility.
I shall not, Mr. Speaker, go into the numerous arguments on both sides. Time does not permit, and they are known to hon. members. Simply, I want to tell you that I have decided to favour the reinstatement of capital punishment for the crime of premeditated, rationally calculated and intentionally committed murder. I do so, not out of a lust for vengeance, not even out of a call for justice-for what is to be gained by revenge, and what justice can there be for the ultimate crime against a member of society? Rather, I call for the reinstatement of capital punishment out of hope-hope that even one innocent life might be saved, that society might be a bit better protected, by the restraint on he who ponders murder of the penalty to which he will be subject.
Capital Punishment
The deterrent effect is the crux of the question. Some state, with absolute sincerity, that capital punishment offers no deterrent effect; others believe, with equal conviction, that it does. The deterrent effect is an uncertain proposition, I readily admit, because one cannot prove it absolutely one way or the other. Nor can we ever lay claim to fully comprehending the actions of any man. However, in full consideration of the information available, and given my limited understanding of human behaviour, I believe that the threat of capital punishment can act as a deterrent to one who in full possession of his mental and physical faculties contemplates cold-blooded murder.
If one wished to get cynical, Mr. Speaker, he might even suggest that it is the deterrent effect of the threat of death that accounts for the success and loyalty to be found for decades in organized crime. A man's greatest temporal possession is his life, and his greatest fear is the loss of that life. That is my belief and the basis of my hope, and that is the reason I want innocent lives given the maximum possible protection. At this time might I just say that the over-all questions of the increase in crime and the need to review our laws and their enforcement are of great concern to me and I hope we shall find it possible to deal further with them during this parliament.
Being in favour of the return of capital punishment I am, of course, opposed to the provision of Bill C-2 as introduced by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). However, it would not be surprising for me to join other retentionists, whatever their reasons, in voting "yea" on second reading so that the bill might be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. This would allow further detailed study and an opportunity for amendment.
If the minister, for whom I have personal regard and respect for his efforts in his department, had introduced a bill for total abolition I would certainly agree to vote so that such bill might receive study in committee. I would, of course, reserve the right to vote against the bill when it returned to the House for third and final reading. However, Mr. Speaker, I can lend no such support to Bill C-2 in its present form-for while the end result of giving this bill second reading would be to have it referred to committee, the vote on second reading is known as approval in principle. I cannot give approval in principle to the furtherance, not even for study, of a bill which I regard as hypocritical.
For one thing, the minister-and, I would predict, almost all of his cabinet colleagues-are abolitionists. Yet they present us with a bill that provides for the death penalty in the case of murder of a prison guard or law enforcement officer. If that alone is not questionable, surely the hypocrisy of this legislation is clear when the government presents us with a proposal it has no intention of carrying out. If a government is unable, or just plain unwilling to carry out legislation, it insults this House by presenting such legislation.

Having put before this House my reason for asking the reinstatement of capital punishment, I wish to acknowledge that I rather doubt that my reason, my fervent but admittedly uncertain hope, will sway the decision of others. subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take advantage of the few minutes allowed to me to express certain opinions on Bill C-2, which is quite simply an extension of the current legislation concerning the death penalty.
I respect the opinions that have been voiced here, and all those that will be expressed by hon. members who speak after me. I think it is important for every member to express his opinion on this bill, and I am glad that there will be a free vote on this matter. Hon. members will thus be able to satisfy the wishes of their constituents and the demands of their consciences.
This bill, which-the term is appropriate-is of capital importance, has been before us for some days, and we all know by now that it was necessary to introduce it, since more than five years have gone by since the legislation at present in force was adopted in 1967. The legislation before us, which is identical to that which existed previously, prescribes hanging for the murder of two sorts of people, prison guards and policemen. I need hardly say that this bill incurs very great responsibility for us, and we must think seriously about all the briefs and communiques that we have received, as well as the statistics provided by the news media and official bodies.
After all this reading, I wished also to know what were the opinions of the constituents whom I represent. And so, a few months ago, I distributed to my constituents a questionnaire on the death penalty, and after receiving
6,000	answers from 83 per cent of my electors I came to the conclusion that they want me to vote in favour of the

retention of capital punishment. I think that I cannot ignore those answers because as federal members of this Parliament it is our duty to respect the feelings of the people who elected us, and I will respect the wish of my electors.
In any case, it so happens that the wish of my electors coincides with my own. I think that some people have been trying for a certain time to inspire sympathy for the hard-core criminal. I am wondering to what extent we as members of this Parliament must let ourselves be influenced by statements from psychiatrists who say that society is always too hard on those who feel free to do anything.
For example, I am thinking about the improvement of our penal institutions. According to some people we must ensure that those criminals have the services which society offers us to the extent we abide by the law. It must be said that the criminal who was sentenced to a number of years in prison deliberately chose to deprive himself of certain liberties.
Perhaps I will now sound cruel by refusing to listen carefully to the advice and recommendations that are often made to improve prisons so as to make them really interesting for those who have to live there. In fact, now and again we hear complaints about the food, the lack of facilities to fill leisure time. I think it must be recognized that the condamned acted deliberately. They have run the risk of not getting caught in the act and, today, I clearly have the impression that people seem to take a little too seriously all these amendments which appear, to some individuals, a priority within our society. Therefore, I may appear somewhat less sympathetic than most to these reforms.
I refer to the professional criminals, because they certainly exist. For all sorts of other reasons, some inmates deserve a certain measure of rehabilitation and attention. There exist, however, some criminals in respect of whom we must take severe action because of the extremely severe action they have personally taken against their fellow human beings.
I should like to insist on prevention. Indeed, people are increasingly inclined to favour parole systems as preventive measures; yet, they must be seriously examined. It would be certainly too late to wait until an individual has reached an advanced age to consider prevention or rehabilitation in his case.
Very objectively speaking, it is the function of the state, I think, to provide for the most expedient implementation of preventive measures.
Therefore, in the present social context, there are shortcomings; one will readily admit that our society is faced with both economic and social problems. These are interrelated and, in certain environments, may result in some individuals becoming criminals because of extremely difficult circumstances.
To what extent can the state improve these difficult environments? How, in the present social context, will we succeed through enforcement of the death penalty in reducing the number of criminals? Hanging itself is certainly not a solution. I think however that, for the hardcore criminal, hanging is a cause of great concern.
May 22, 1973

The criminal who did not hesite to kill his neighbour to carry out his aim deserves a similar treatment. Endlessly repeating "Thou shalt not kill" is not a deterrent. Did the murderer also think about those words? And in the present social context, for instance, if we only reinstate capital punishment without thinking of other solutions which could possibly decrease the number of murderers, we will certainly be wrong. I am one of those who believe that the killer must suffer the same fate as his victim. Others, for all kinds of reasons, think differently.
We are dealing with a bill introduced by the government; all members are still free to express their views about this bill. We all know very well that the bill specified hanging for two categories of person.
We must recognize that capital punishment has not been applied for five years and I am concerned and disappointed. And we know also that the bill before the House calls for the suspension of capital punishment for five more years except for the death of prison guards and police officers. And until now the government has not taken a firm position against capital punishment. Does that mean that criminals responsible for the death of prison guards or police officers would have the advantage of having their death sentence commuted to life imprisonment? In view of the statements made this afternoon by a number of government members, we must ask ourselves some questions while evaluating the bill before us. If we are against hanging, we can absolutely not support this bill. If we are for the maintenance of capital punishment, we cannot support this bill either. Therefore, this bill is clearly inadequate and from our passed experience it is obvious that the former law was violated even though it was adopted on a free vote five years ago. I regret the government did not respect, as the House wished, a law which has been adopted in a most democratic way.
I would remind the House that 83 per cent of my constituents have participated in a poll made in my riding. I would like to invite the House to give special attention to what might be called the correction of a social climate. It has been demonstrated-and we realize this through various organizations and commissions-that our social context includes what we call underprivileged classes where people live under difficult conditions. To what extent is it possible for a government or a Parliament to set up organizations or commissions responsible for implementing a prevention system? I think we have much to do in this field and, once more, I will not insist by blaming the government. However, as members of Parliament, we should see to it that this prevention system be implemented so as to prevent an ever increasing number of people from taking inadmissible liberties, whatever their motives.
I think it is incumbent upon us to set up organizations which could improve considerably our social climate. We are perfectly aware as well of the fact-and we admit it- that 30 per cent of the people live in poverty. Certainly, in such conditions, there are people who do not have what we call the vital minimum and, therefore, if we do not correct this injustice, if we do not improve social conditions, we might experience difficult times when it comes to crimi-
Capital Punishment
nality. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we must seriously consider deterrents.
As for parole, many people have spoken about it. We know the results of some experiments that took place; it is out of question, of course, to release on parole a criminal recognized as such. However, there are groups of criminals who have committed quite serious crimes, but not the most serious, and who surely deserve special consideration for rehabilitation. I suggest that it is our responsibility to enable these groups of criminals to be rehabilitated, but we must first proceed with a careful screening.
In my opinion, we should give priority to all possible deterrents which would eliminate at the same time the need for rehabilitation.
Of course, our law enables the accused to defend themselves. It is quite normal, in a civilized society, that criminals be able to defend themselves. We often come to wonder whether a given crime was premeditated or not. We must not hesitate to bring back capital punishment for so-called hired guns. We are perfectly aware that there is a group of people who, for a few hundred dollars, do not hesitate to kill somebody, and the real criminal, as a rule, is not quite he who commits the crime. Nevertheless, the indivudual who decides to take someone's life must expect the state to take action to protect society and to ensure respect of the right to life. And I believe the paid killer should expect no sympathetic treatment from justice.
I also have in mind the man who does not hesitate to commit a bank robbery, or to gun down either a teller or a policeman. We will often be told, of course, that he did not intend to kill. Why, then, did he enter a bank after taking good care to load his weapon?
My opinion is quite clear on that point: the same man could carry out his robbery without necessarily loading his weapon. If his intention is only to frighten the teller, he will achieve it. But if he goes to the trouble of loading his gun, I believe he accepts the idea of killing in case it should become necessary, and in my opinion it is evident that if he foresaw that it might be necessary to kill in order to succeed in his venture, we are dealing with a criminal who has no right to freedom.
In the underworld, there is no reluctance to use a gun and I believe it is the government's responsibility to protect society against this group of people who, as we well know, have leverage in many places. I feel the mafia should not escape severe justice and that we should therefore not hesitate to restore the death penalty, at the least for murders of policemen and prison gards. There are other categories of murderers who, for debatable reasons, may win some sympathy either from the court or the public.
For about ten years now, we have been dealing with drug users. In some minds, it is clear that whoever, for some reason or other, takes a small dose of drugs, is not responsible for the carnage he may provoke. Still, it is surprising that the same man should be able to go to the address he was given to commit his crime. Some will be tempted to prove, by all sorts of means, that he was not aware of what he was doing; yet, he committed his crime perfectly. I therefore have many reservations about whoever justifies himself by claiming that he was drunk or

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
under the influence of some drug or other, and who therefore is not responsible for his act.
Let me return again to a wider use of preventive measures. It is important for parliament to set up a mechanism whereby young people can, at early age, be withdrawn from an unwholesome environment, conducive to making of him a hardened criminal.
We know that with the parole system, some criminals may serve a certain number of years in jail and then be released. The people are very much concerned about this and I have had the opportunity of getting several opinions on this from the public. I have read the brief presented by the police association which is very much concerned about the freedom that is being granted to some dangerous criminals. And we recognize more and more that guards and policemen are worried about the release of certain dangerous criminals. I think that this should make us show much more severity toward these criminals.
They will try and justify themselves with statistics. What is the use of statistics when one is faced with crimes such as those we have seen these past few years? For those who believe that the death penalty is not a deterrent, I repeat that it gives the most hardened criminal cause for reflection and I think that for the one who took the liberty of killing his neighbour, there is no other punishment than that of death penalty.
The recent escapes may have been found more or less funny. I think that the department concerned must quickly undertake the investigation which it requested and find who is responsible for those escapes. I would not dare say that the minister must be held responsible for those escapes, surely not. I know the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and his great sincerity. However, we find it very strange how easily some prisoners recently escaped. I think that the investigation should be held as soon as possible and that we must ask serious questions about the management of our prisons. I imagine that the inquiry will bring us sufficient evidence to show that there are guilty parties in the prisons; as for those outside, I know nothing about them. One thing is sure, however; offenders should be severely reprehended and escapes have become a joke among people as well as a most serious and alarming problem. They should end as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make these few remarks because I consider the legislation under consideration quite important. I believe that as members we should take part in this debate and express our views. In fact, it is important that the opinions held in our various regions should be made known in the House. There will always remain this basic question: Why and how does one become a criminal? I think this will be the everlasting question for us to ask ourselves every day and that the state's task is to spare nothing in order to set up these prevention and rehabilitation systems whenever the latter is possible.
The government and Parliament have the responsibility to severely punish whoever abuses individual freedom. Therefore, it is quite clear that I shall vote against this bill which is the repetition of a law that we have had. Being dissatisfied with the legislation already passed, I could not honestly support the bill that is before us now.

And if this bill is to be defeated, I shall be only too happy about it because I believe in the reinstatement of capital punishment for the criminal who does not stop at anything to make his wishes come true by any means. And I trust that Parliament will continue to try and set up prevention services which would also reduce the number of criminals. To the extent where the social climate is improved, their number will be reduced. To my mind, we have a great deal to do to set up various institutions in order that these corrective measures be applicable and applied as soon as possible.
In conclusion, I would like to say once again that I admit that it is not only by reinstating capital punishment that we will improve our society, but through the implementation of several corrective measures. If the responsible departments use a great deal of imagination, if the social climate is improved, we may at last reduce the number of criminals. I am convinced that the criminal who deliberately commits murder must be severely punished and that means the death penalty.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this now rather agonizing debate because of my own moral conviction that capital punishment serves only to wreak social vengeance on the one hand, and brutalize our entire penal system on the other. Although I believe in total abolition, I am prepared to support Bill C-2 which calls for a further extension of the trial period of abolition of capital punishment except in cases relating to the murder of policemen or prison guards as defined in the Criminal Code.
For those who would argue on fundamentalist grounds that the noose should be brought back, I can only say that it is my belief that the Christian ethic of love and forgiveness precludes the taking of a life for a life. In my opinion, one act of violence does not in any way call for or demand another act of violence. In the past decade we have seen, on a global scale, violence beyond imagination where legal murder in the name of war and political idealogy has wiped out many thousands of lives. We have lived through a violent decade. Must we continue, through capital murder, the destruction of human life?
I am not a bleeding-heart when it comes to sympathizing with a convicted murder who in cold blood and full knowledge of his act has taken the life of an innocent person. But what advantage is gained in legally murdering the perpetrator of a crime, no matter how useless a human being the convicted slayer might be? To me, capital punishment is morally and socially debasing. It appeals to the lower animal instincts of revenge and retribution, totally disregarding the years of effort, study and the practice of rehabilitation on the part of those dedicated to improving the dignity of even our most anti-social citizens. How can you rehabilitate a dead person?
This latter view is particularly cogent when one considers the following statistics, although I am aware of the fact that in this particular debate statistics can be misleading. Between 1920 and 1967, 151 persons who had been sentenced to death in Canada had their sentences commuted and were subsequently paroled. Of this number, 92
May 22, 1973

were successful in that they were never returned to prison on any charge. This experience is similar to the experience in the United States in respect of recidivism related to parole. The recidivism rate of paroled murders is very low.
It is interesting to note that of all types of criminals, most murderers, with the exception of the mentally ill, are the most responsive to rehabilitation. Indeed, experience has indicated that a majority of persons convicted of murder are not criminals in the sense that they earn their living from crime but, rather, are involved in a crime of passion, often of a domestic nature, and their violent act is a once in a lifetime matter. Such persons often can be safely and usefully released back into society long before 25 years. Some members have proposed a 25-year imprisonment period, which is totally unacceptable to me personally because we would be lumping all convicted murderers into one group. Some, obviously, cannot be rehabilitated in 10 or 15 years, and perhaps some never.
I wish to emphasize that I am not referring to convicted murders who fall into the general category of the criminally insane, the sexual psychopath and the hardened criminal. In fact, we must tighten our parole and pass system to ensure that such criminals do not gain even temporary freedom until fully cured, if indeed they can be cured at all. If the latter is the case, and unfortunately it is in most cases, then society must be protected and they must be denied their freedom even if it means for a lifetime. It is my opinion that inmates who are incapable of parole should not be left to rot behind bars but, under very controlled circumstances, should be put to work in gainful employment contributing in some way to the development of this country. For example, why not put them to work in various parts of the country building highways, bridges or airfields, or put them to any other gainful employment?
For those who argue for the retention of the death penalty on grounds of the deterrent factor, a great deal already has been said. Impressive arguments for and against the effectiveness of capital punishment in deterring others from committing murder have been made, and statistics have been used and abused. Murderers usually fall into three main categories: the person, otherwise law abiding, who in a fit of passion kills a person without premeditation; the mentally ill or the psychopath; and the hardened criminal whose life of crime one day results in murder, premeditated or otherwise.
Jealousy, greed and emotional instability are difficult to control by those so afflicted although they live useful lives within the law. To what extent does the threat of the death penalty deter those caught up in passion and rage? I suggest there is no deterrent factor here at all. Let us keep in mind that this first category comprises the vast majority of murderers. Also in this group are those who kill as a result of being in a state of intoxication or under the effects of drugs, or a combination of both.
Does capital punishment deter the mentally ill? Again I suggest the answer is no. The only real deterrent here is cure through medical science, which unfortunately is woefully ill-equipped to handle such persons in our mental institutions today due to insufficient funds for research,
Capital Punishment
lack of staff due to inadequate salaries compared to those of psychiatrists who work in a free enterprise system and, as a consequence, difficult working conditions for the personnel who have the courage and dedication to enter upon such difficult careers. Trying to cure the criminally insane today is a horrendous undertaking, and I suggest that governments at all levels must drastically improve the situation.
We come now to the hardened criminal. In most cases these people come from socially deprived backgrounds; not always, but usually. They often come from broken homes where a sense of human dignity and the worth of the individual are virtually non-existent. They have been battered and bruised both physically and emotionally for years-unfortunately, the young, impressionable years. They develop anti-social attitudes and a complete disrespect for authority. They turn to crime because they have no respect for their fellow human beings. They have no sense of human involvement or community involvement. Society is to be paid back for what society has done to them in the form of neglect, poverty or rejection: at least, this is their attitude. It may be a warped attitude, but it is their attitude.
Does capital punishment deter this kind of criminal? It might in some instances, but statistics neither prove nor disprove that the threat of being hanged enters a hardened criminal's mind on the way to the bank with a loaded pistol that results in the death of the manager or some innocent bystander.
Professor Fattah, in "A Study of the deterrent effect of capital punishment with special reference to the Canadian situation", concludes that the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent is so limited that its abolition cannot have any serious effect on the incidence of murder. He cites the following limits of deterrence: first, deterrence is irrelevant to the bulk of the population which follows the normal norms of society and whose self-concepts will not permit them to commit crimes. I am referring to the conclusions in his report.
Second, deterrence cannot be effective in the case of certain acts of an impulsive nature where high emotions or strong motivations are involved. Third, deterrence cannot be effective for certain categories of criminals such as insane, abnormal, impulsive or compulsive offenders or those consciously or unconsciously seeking to be punished. Fourth, the death penalty cannot be an effective deterrent for those who are not afraid to die or those who have a conscious or unconscious desire to die. This includes murderers who commit suicide. Fifth, deterrence cannot be effective in cases where punishment can be avoided.
The error of the deterrence theory can also be shown statistically with reference to the United States. Now that several states have had no death penalty for several years, it is possible to compare some neighbouring states with similar populations and educational and economic levels, some with and some without capital punishment. For example, Rhode Island, without capital punishment, has a consistently lower murder rate in proportion to the total population than its neighbours, Connecticut and Massachusetts which do have capital punishment.
Similarly, Michigan, without capital punishment, has a better record than Indiana or Ohio both of which have

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
capital punishment. Wisconsin, without capital punishment, has a better record than Iowa or Minnesota which do have capital punishment. If all the states are compared, the murder rate is from two to three times greater in the states which have and enforce the death penalty than in those that do not.
This by no means proves that abolishing the death penalty will reduce the crime rate by one half, but it does prove that other considerations-social, economic, educational, racial-have far more to do with deterring or favouring crime than does the kind of punishment called for by the law.
If the retentionists are really convinced that capital punishment is in fact a deterrent to the commission of murder, then I wonder why hangings are held in secret, in the middle of the night, and not in the market square in public, complete with colour television cameras. I know this has been said before, but it should be repeated: once hangings were done in public-without the cameras, of course-but we still had murder.
The Ontario Association of Professional Social Workers argues that the issue of the death penalty is really one of ethics and morality. I quote their words:
As social workers, we feel that the worth and dignity of man is cheapened and lessened by state execution. We are in strong support of abolishing the death penalty.
The association goes on to say:
We believe that there are more important issues than the issue of capital punishment, such as the inadequacy of current rehabilitation schemes and the need for effective programs in combating the causes of crime.
This brings me to the crunch of the whole argument as I see it. It is my opinion that due to the obvious increase in the crime rate as a whole, the general public, concerned about public safety and protection as they should be, are confusing the death penalty as a deterrent to murder with the death penalty as a deterrent to all serious crimes. In other words, bring back hanging and we will have fewer bank robberies, muggings, crimes of breaking and entering, and so on. This is a fallacious argument, in my opinion. While the crime rate has gone up in recent years, the murder rate has not gone up at a corresponding rate; in fact, Statistics Canada report that in the year 1972 the crime rate in Canada actually declined slightly.
I mentioned earlier that we must get tougher with first and second offenders while they are still young and at least potentially responsive to proper rehabilitation. We must also make sure that dangerous inmates are not prematurely released back into society to pose a threat to life and property. We must continue with an enlightened parole system based on successful rehabilitation, provided that the authorities are not lax in the screening processes they have developed. If a person is given a life sentence, and if he cannot be rehabilitated, then his freedom to mix in society must be permanently curtailed. We must tackle the social, economic and educational problems which create and promote criminality.
The increase in the murder rate in the last five years was the lowest among all crimes of violence, a fact that indicates that such increase can be neither attributed nor
related to suspension of capital punishment. The increase in murder is part of a general increase in criminal violence. Most murderers are not responsible for their crimes in a vacuum; all of us in Canadian society must share the responsibility because we allow conditions of poverty, exploitation and discrimination to exist in the context in which murder takes place.
I call on hon. members to vote for Bill C-2, to give their support to another five-year trial period in the hope that more evidence at the end of that time will unquestionably show that the state taking a life for a life is not a deterrent, or at least an effective deterrent to murder. If Luxemburg could abolish the death penalty in 1822, Belgium in 1863, Portugal in 1867, Holland in 1870 and Brazil in 1891, then surely we in Canada can support this bill extending the moratorium on hanging in the hope that at the end of the new trial period we will abolish capital punishment forever.
Some speakers in this debate have made reference to the growth of violence. Unfortunately, we live beside a nation which from its very origin has to some degree almost boasted about the law of the gun. I am not anti-American when I say this, but for generations the gun has been law in certain parts of the United States. And yet we have had hanging in the United States, we have had the gas chamber, we have had electrocution: until recently we had the death penalty in 39 of the 50 states. It is true that in the last two or three years they have not been putting people to death, but up until five years ago some states were putting convicted murderers to death; yet the crime rate increased.
Unfortunately for law-abiding Americans, the American city today is no longer safe. I ask those who are retentionists to reflect upon this point, that that country in its major cities has become a violent nation. Yet for generations, indeed for centuries, it put people to death for murder and for other acts of violence. And we still have this growing crime rate.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the retentionists that hanging in the United States has not worked as a deterrent. It is possibly the best example of any country in the world where hanging, or the death penalty in general, has not worked as a deterrent. I think that should be adequate proof that at least this bill to extend the moratorium on capital punishment should be passed on second reading.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the many speeches made in this House and I feel that by now we have aired all the views both pro and con. Consequently, it is my intention to make my remarks brief and of a general nature only. It is my opinion, having discussed the question of capital punishment over the years and listening to the speeches made in this House, that it is virtually impossible to convert a confirmed abolitionist into a retentionist or to convert a confirmed retentionist into an abolitionist. Both have arguments to support their views, both are sincere and both are able to adduce statistics to support their arguments.
Bill C-2 which we are debating today has the effect of placing a moratorium on the death penalty for a further

May 22, 1973

period of five years except as it relates to the murder of police officers and prison guards or officials. We are being asked to extend the ban after a five-year trial period because, in the words of the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand), the government does not have the full data for the whole of the previous five years. He said in the debate in this House on January 26, as reported at page 688 of Hansard:
Statistics are some two years behind and therefore at the moment we are only in possession of full data covering the first three years of the trial period.
I find that statement hard to accept in this age of computers. Surely the government, being aware of the fact that there was need to deal with this matter on or before December 30, 1972, could have given top priority to the compilation of statistics in order to have the information available to this House. But supposing we did have the statistics, Mr. Speaker-what would they prove? I suggest they would prove nothing, because since 1962 no person has been hanged in Canada. In effect, there has been no capital punishment in Canada since 1962. Since 1968 there have been four convictions for the murder of police officers and the government has commuted their death sentences.
After listening to the remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this House on January 30 last, I can appreciate the heavy responsibility that is placed upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of his cabinet when faced with the decision of whether or not a sentence of death should be commuted. But I find it hard to believe that the circumstances surrounding all murders since 1962 have warranted commutation.
There is great concern amongst responsible citizens in Canada as to the direction in which our society is going. They are concerned about the safety of their families, and well they should be under present circumstances where bail procedures are such that potentially dangerous criminals are allowed out on bail to commit further crimes, where weekend passes from prison are almost a right rather than a privilege, and where prison breaks in Canada are almost a weekly occurrence.
It is the responsibility of the government and of this House to take steps to make certain that society is protected and that citizens are able to live without fear of violence. How does a government assume this responsibility? Mr. Speaker, it assumes it by passing the legislation which makes certain that we have law and order in our country, laws which provide the rules by which we live and penalties that are punitive in nature and will deter an individual from breaking the law.
It is a further responsibility of a government to see to it that the law is enforced and that the sentences handed down by the courts are carried out. The extent of the punishment depends upon the seriousness of the crime. There is no point in having the same punishment for robbing a parking meter of a few dollars as there is for robbing a bank at gun point of $10,000. Therefore, we must have punishment which fits the crime in that the punishment must be of such a nature that it will act as a deterrent.
Capital Punishment
There is no greater crime than the taking of another's life. It has long been recognized, however, where a person was insane at the time of commission of the crime and did not know the nature and consequences of his act, that he was not guilty of murder. It has been recognized that killing in self-defence is not murder. It has been further recognized that people, being human and having emotions, at times due to aggravation, are unable to control their emotions and kill one another. This is not necessarily murder, depending upon the degree of aggravation.
Mr. Speaker, in instances where someone deliberately and with premeditation kills another, that is murder. It is also murder when a person kills someone in the commission of a crime, for in these instances he knows what he is doing and must be held accountable. If he is prepared to knowingly assume the risk, he must also assume the consequences if we are to have law and order.
In my opinion, there is no distinction between the killing of a policeman or a prison official or the killing of a private citizen. It is a life of an individual, not the life of a person in a particular occupation that is important. It is my opinion that capital punishment should be extended to those persons who kidnap another and hold them for ransom in fear of their lives, or those persons who hijack an aircraft and endanger the lives of the passengers. This, Mr. Speaker, is the stand I took throughout the election campaign and a conviction I have held for a number of years. It is not based on any poll that I took of my constituents, or on public opinion.
I know that the abolitionists will say that capital punishment is revenge on the part of society, but I ask them: Is it revenge to spank a child when he misbehaves? Is it revenge to send a man to jail for robbing a bank, or to fine him for speeding? It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that a man who commits murder has forfeited his right to live and remain as a part of our society.
I was disappointed to hear the hon. Solicitor General in the closing part of his argument recite some of the gory details of execution, possibly in an atttempt to emotionally shock retentionists into changing their opinion about capital punishment. I did not hear him speak of the victim or the families of victims. Perhaps he has not spoken, as I have, with members of families who lost a son or a daughter as a result of murder, or to a woman who was present when her husband was murdered. Perhaps he has not given thought to the terror experienced by a young female child or young woman who was sexually assaulted before being violently beaten to death.
With respect to the method of execution, I am not satisfied that hanging or the gas chamber or electrocution is the means by which the death penalty should be carried out, because surely in this day and age there must be a more sophisticated means of putting a person to death. It is the fear of death, not the method of death, that is the deterrent.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we live in a democratic society, one in which the government must express the will of the people. I do not feel that simply because I was able to win an election and come to Ottawa as a Member of Parliament that I have suddenly become more knowledgeable

May 22, 1973
Capital Punishment
than my constituents when it comes to making a decision on what I believe is basically a moral matter. The Gallup polls have indicated that an overwhelming majority of people in Canada believe in capital punishment. That is the will of the people; that is democracy. If the abolitionists who are in the minority can satisfy the majority that capital punishment is wrong, then it will be abolished. But let us not, as representatives of the people, be swayed by emotion or by statistics which are inconclusive.
Mr. Speaker, it is therefore my intention to vote against this bill.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject of abolition of capital punishment has been under debate in this House for at least the past two decades. I have just listened to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) express his viewpoint and I recall that it was an earlier member for Moose Jaw who introduced the private member's resolution for the original debate in this House on the abolition of capital punishment. I refer, of course, to the late Ross Thatcher who once was the member for Moose Jaw. At that time the abolitionists were outright abolitionists and you had a clearcut decision when the vote came before parliament. In response to the debate during that decade, the government of the day moved forward with legislation which again gave Members of Parliament a firm legislative basis upon which they could make a decision.
The government of the day back in 1961, I think it was, introduced legislation which divided the crime of homicide into two distinct categories, capital and non-capital. That was the legislation that applied until the more murky decade of the 1960s when the element of uncertainty, which hovers over this debate tonight as it has during the whole period the matter has been under discussion, was introduced. We are not debating abolition, and we are not debating retention tonight; we are debating a compromise piece of legislation which would retain capital punishment, for reasons that can only be known to the government, for two isolated instances of homicide.
As a matter of fact, we are back to the legislation of 1961^because the trial period that began in 1967 expired at the beginning of the year and we are now operating under the legislation of the two distinct categories, capital and non-capital murder. It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that the compromise legislation of the government only tends to confuse the issue.
I think there is a much more important issue which demands the attention of this House, otherwise we are going to lose the progress we have made in the field of the rehabilitative approach to the handling of crime in Canada and we are not going to settle the very difficult issue of capital punishment. The atmosphere and the mood, as I have listened to the debates in this House of Commons and as I have read the editorial comments in the newspapers across the nation, refer to the fact that because of the breakdown in our penal system it is impossible for either parliamentarians or the people of Canada to make a clearcut decision on this matter at the moment. The issue we should be discussing, and which will be considering in committee when the committee starts functioning, is the whole question of penal reform.
[Mr. Neil.l
As the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) himself has indicated, our prisons are overcrowded and rehabilitation programs are inadequate. As we know, the inevitable result has been the increase of breakouts, which have been referred to by hon. members and which have brought our penitentiary system into disrepute during the past few weeks.
I would also remind the Solicitor General that there is a piece of legislation that is fundamentally important to rehabilitation but is being left in a state of suspension. I refer to the government's attempt to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which fell by the wayside one year ago. It was withdrawn and has not yet reappeared on the order paper. If there is any period in life when it is more important than in any other period to deal with the rehabilitative approach to crime, to recidivism and to all the other problems associated with lawbreaking in this country, it is the juvenile years when there is some hope for bringing about reform and in redirecting the lifestyle and personality of young Canadians.
It is tragic that Parliament is being forced day after day to discuss an issue which from the standpoint of retention or abolition is to some extent phony. Even the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), when he spoke the other day, said that he is an outright abolitionist but will be forced to vote for this bill which is partly retentionist.
My recommendation, Mr. Speaker, is that we remain where we are at the moment. At least Members of Parliament will know where they stand, and at least the people of Canada will know where we stand. The legislation which provides for capital and non-capital categories of murder makes it possible for the courts of this country, under our system of jurisprudence to exercise a rehabilitative approach in cases of non-capital categories which involve unpremeditated murder, and so on. On the other hand, the law makes it possible for the courts-that is, the judges of Canada-to exercise their responsibilities, and surely they have responsibilities under our system of jurisprudence, and decide what categories of crime shall come under the capital murder category.
At present we are living in an era of moral confusion and uncertainty in this country. That may be the reason for the government's fuzzy thinking on this issue. There are murderers, perpetrators of homicide who will not respond to rehabilitation under any circumstances. The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) dealt with one such specific instance in his contribution to the debate this afternoon. Some murderers are placed in the category of psychopaths. They have no sense of values, no conscience, and murder with impunity. Their existence, I think, reflects the fact that we live in a society that is confused and morally sick.
Many editorials have appeared on the subject. One appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 22 of this year. An article on rehabilitation under the byline of Jackson Toby referred to the fact that some criminals will never respond to any attempt at rehabilitation because of their childhood circumstances and experience. There is the childhood of the unwanted child, the slow learner in school, the stigmatized child in the neighbourhood. When these people grow up they are incapable of rehabilitation
May 22, 1973

because they have developed what the psychologists call a psychopathic personality. Those are the categories to which the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) referred this afternoon. No prison, no probation, no psychiatrist can provide a new childhood, said Mr. Jackson Toby, and anything but a new childhood is too late in dealing with this category. Perhaps that is why the founder of Christianity referred to the new birth as the only solution to behaviour of this kind, and why modern psychology is working on the whole question of behaviour modification.
Scandinavia has recognized the problem and has now resorted to what it calls internment, which is long deprivation of liberty without duration fixed in advance. In other words, for the psychopathic personality involved in homicide there is indeterminate sentencing. Internment is their treatment of the crime, in place of capital punishment.
One of the reasons for moral breakdown, of course, is that there is breakdown in the basic institutions of our society. The family, which should be the healing place of the soul, has become the breeding ground for juvenile deliquency, divorce and all the other problems which beset the modern family. I think we are all aware that the late Governor General, Georges Vanier, and Madam Vanier instituted the Vanier Institute of the Family to deal with this fundamental problem in our society.
Our schools are having the same difficulty. As someone has said, and oversimplified, in addition to teaching the three R's, our youngsters are being taught the fourth R, that of rebellion. The problem is reflected in some of the legislative initiatives of this government, inasmuch as the permissive legislation of recent years has reflected the moral decline of society. Several members have said during this debate that to resort to capital punishment even for the heinous kinds of crime that have been referred to, even for murder performed by the psychopathic personality who has no moral compunction, is to brutalize society and lessen respect for life.
To show the moral confusion that this reflects, let me say, as I think we are aware, particularly since the Alliance for Life was in Ottawa some two years ago, that the so-called therapeutic abortion legislation in effect means on demand. This indicates an absolute disrespect for life inasmuch as thousands of unborn human beings can have their very lives terminated in the name of therapeutic abortion. When the Alliance for Life was in Ottawa it referred to the moral crisis of the nurses who have to gather the dismembered bodies of those children. They referred to the slaughter of the innocents. That indicates how life has become brutalized and how confused we are in our moral concepts. On the one hand we defend the right of the psychopathic criminal to life, and on the other hand we deny the right to life to the innocents who are now being eliminated by the thousands in what, in effect, is abortion on demand.
Murder is the ultimate crime. I am not going to argue the problem on religious grounds because you can get theologians to argue on both sides of the question. There is a phrase that I think is appropriate, that man was made in the image of God. When someone commits murder against his fellow man, that creature made in the image of God is
Capital Punishment
destroyed. It is the ultimate crime. In some instances it deserves the ultimate penalty.
As society has progressed there has been a gradual elimination of the death penalty. I only wish that in the society in which we live Canada could go for complete abolition. This is not possible. This was determined back in the fifties by legislation of that day. The government in its wisdom has concluded that it is not possible to do so because it retains capital punishment for the murder of prison guards and police officers.
This House would much better use the time at its disposal by dealing with urgent issues awaiting the consideration of hon. members, leaving this matter where it stands with capital and non-capital murder. The safety of the state would be assured in cases of syndicated crime, the Mafia sort of homicide, hijacking, treason, murders carried out in cold blood by individuals who in many instances are psychopathic.
I am not going to argue from the standpoint of deterrence. That is beside the point, because social scientists can quote statistics on both sides. I argue that there is something in mankind; as the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) said the other day when quoting Pasternak, there is a beast lurking in every human heart. The same thought is expressed by the concept of the id lurking in the murky labyrinth of the subconscious which is supposed to bubble to the surface and cause the perpetration of all sorts of heinous crimes. I am talking about the Christian concept of human nature which says that the heart of man is desperately wicked beyond all human understanding. Here is the situation, in human nature, in the moral confusion of society at the present time that has brought about the growing feeling of concern and anxiety of an increasing number of people in Canada.
Let us get on with the task of dealing with the breakdown of our penal system. Let us get on with the task of a comprehensive examination of the growing problem of crime and violence. Punishment is something we must retain in our criminal system unless we are going to make the whole system meaningless. Whether that punishment be life imprisonment, capital punishment or a different penalty, we have at the moment legislation that is adequate to deal with the problem as reflected in the expressed concern of thousands of Canadians across this country who want to see capital punishment retained for certain crimes and eliminated for others.
Let us carry on with the business of the nation, and not compound and confuse the issue with the half-baked legislation before us. Some will vote for the legislation as retentionists, some will vote against it as retentionists, some will vote for it as abolitionists and others will vote against it. Nothing will be settled; we will be back where we started. The problem of penal reform is much more important.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-STUDY ON DECENTRALIZATION OF OFFICES-PUBLICATION OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on two different occasions I directed questions to the attention of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) relating to the administrative costs of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. These were on March 7 and March 16 of this year. At that time I asked whether there was a blitz on in the department against administrative efficiency and excessive expenditures to correspond with legislation presently in effect whereby claimants were being given a hard time with regard to their UIC benefits. I do not wish to be quarrelsome this evening but there are a few points I wish to raise in connection with the administrative costs of the unemployment insurance program.
There has been a great deal of verbiage this session about the various ramifications of Governor General's warrants and other aspects of the unemployment insurance program. However, little has been said in this House about the horrendous increase in costs and the great problems of inefficiency that have been manifested to those who have studied what has gone on in this department in the past few years.
I want to raise just a few points. First, I wish to protest against the administrative costs that have resulted in the misguided attempt to restructure the unemployment Insurance Commission. According to my information, two or three years ago the administrative costs were in the vicinity of $43 million to $46 million. At that time the committee and the public were told that when computers and decentralization were brought in regional pay offices and the so-called improvements, they would result in benefits to the claimant and the taxpayer. Unfortunately, this has not been the case.
Recent news items and news releases indicate that in this administrative year the commission is going to spend $14 million to put the service back to where it was in 1971 before district offices started being closed. The real scandal is that it is now costing in the vicinity of $145 million for administrative costs, whereas a couple of years ago this cost the taxpayers of Canada between $43 million and $46 million.
What has happened is that in many areas of Canada there has been great hardship. My constituency is only one

of several areas where people have had to spend a great deal of money and go to a great deal of trouble in order to receive the service they once received as a matter of course. The former national employment service was not bad in that respect. One of its architects was Tom Kent, at that time an eminence gris in this venerable place.
