He won
his war on poverty.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-STUDY ON DECENTRALIZATION OF OFFICES-PUBLICATION OF REPORT
speechtext:
He was the man who came out with the concept of a national manpower strategy. This has been nothing less than a disaster. What has happened is that labour unions, claimants and all those affected by the Unemployment Insurance Commission have borne the brunt as far as the organization of the UIC is concerned. The ridiculous part is that after causing a lot of misery to the people of Canada, the government is spending $14 million to put back what they took away only a few months ago.
I want restoration of the type of service once provided for my constituents. I say this as a result of many complaints and representations made to me by labour unions and by people who have legitimate complaints to make against the UIC. My complaints-I want to make this clear-in no way reflect upon the efficiency or the cooperative spirit with which the UIC staff has acted in the terrible situation which has been foisted upon them by those who are supposedly in control of the department. The Halifax regional office and, indeed, the New Glasgow regional office have done their best in individual cases to bring satisfaction to individuals who have been adversely affected by government policies. But the way in which administrative costs have gone up by millions of dollars, at the same time as service to the client has degenerated, is nothing less than a national scandal. There has been a complete failure of planning and, as a consequence, unnecessary work has come to the attention of Members of Parliament in all parties.
I hope the government has learned a lesson from this colossal blunder involving the administration of the UIC. I take pleasure in stating that unless some effort is made to put the blame where it belongs, that is, on the senior officials of the department, the government will encounter even greater difficulty in obtaining co-operation from Members of Parliament. The minister has requested hon. members to put forward suggestions. He has asked that we be patient. But unless the government pays attention to the situation it is creating as a result of these bureaucratic blunders, it will receive no co-operation either from the people of Canada or from those directly affected. The way the government has administered the affairs of the UIC amounts to nothing less than a disaster.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-STUDY ON DECENTRALIZATION OF OFFICES-PUBLICATION OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just come from a meeting of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration at which colleagues of the hon. member closely questioned my minister on these very matters. My answer here must naturally be much more summary than that which my minister was able to make before the committee.
May 22, 1973

I am advised that a special report prepared after implementation of computerization concluded that in 1970-71 the Commission realized a saving of $1,841,000, based on the 1967-68 manual operation. The reason for the increase in costs is therefore other than the institution of the computerization program. In actual fact, administrative costs for 1971 and 1972 were as follows: the costs for 1971 amounted to $86,098,000; for 1972 the cost was $122,174,000; and the estimated cost for 1973 is $145,163,000.
Starting in 1970, increases in the workload and major operational changes resulting from the introduction of the new act have caused expansion of the regional facilities. The increase in program administration costs is due to a number of factors. Escalating costs, such as salary increases, accommodation, rental costs, postal rate increases and the elimination of mailing privileges have affected the administrative expenditures. Increased costs have also been incurred in providing improvements in service to the public through a more personalized approach in dealing with claimants and the decentralization of the commission's operations. In addition, the increase in the workload I have already noted has resulted in the need to increase the staff complement to a level commensurate with that workload.
Last year the commission responded to 13 million inquiries, handled 2.5 million claims and made 17 million benefit payments. These are impressive figures indeed, and when we put up against them the fact that only in a fairly small number of cases were there problems on the part of claimants, problems that we are doing our best to remedy, we realize that the system is working very well.
If we had thought it was working perfectly, we would not have felt it necessary to implement the changes that were recently brought into effect. However, I assure the hon. member that the commission itself is making every effort to provide the best possible service, and the new system of decentralization which is being instituted we believe will ensure an even better service than has been the case in the past two or three years.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BRUCELLOSIS-REQUEST THAT COMPENSATION TO FARMERS BE EQUATED WITH FAIR MARKET VALUE-SUGGESTED VACCINATION PROGRAM
AGRICULTURE-BRUCELLOSIS-REQUEST THAT COMPENSATION TO FARMERS BE EQUATED WITH FAIR MARKET VALUE-SUGGESTED VACCINATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked a series of questions last Thursday, May 17, and also on the following day, regarding Bang's disease, more scientifically known as brucellosis, which has occurred in northern Saskatchewan. Some of the answers that the minister gave me at that time were quite satisfactory, although I think some of them were slightly evasive and not too satisfactory so far as some of my constituents are concerned. It is unfortunate that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is not in the chamber; he was here until a few minutes ago.
Saskatchewan was a Bang's-free area until several years ago. During the 1950s there was a program of extensive vaccination of cows or heifers against Bang's disease. This program was dropped by the federal government in the late 1950s and early 1960s in favour of eradication of the disease by eliminating reactors. Some veterinarians now tell us-there seems to be some conflict here among
Adjournment Debate
veterinarians-that cows are not suitable for the export market if they have been vaccinated against this disease because they can show up as reactors or give a positive result when tested. On the other hand, I hear from good sources that many states in the United States do not accept imported cattle unless they have been vaccinated. I am told that the only countries in the world that do not accept cattle vaccinated against Bang's are countries like Japan and Russia.
In addition to the questions I asked the minister last Thursday, there are several other questions that I want to pose to him tonight in response to points raised at a meeting held in the area of Big River, Saskatchewan, in my constituency, by a group of farmers who are very concerned about the spread of this disease. There have been cases of this disease in the area around Prince Albert, Debden, Victoire, Big River, Meadow Lake and Pierceland. This covers an area of about 200 miles from Prince Albert to the Alberta border. It also extends south and north of this line.
Some of the farmers whose animals have been affected by this disease made the following suggestions at a number of meetings they have held in the past several weeks. I would like the minister, or his parliamentary secretary, to reply to some of these suggestions. First of all, it is felt that the Animal Contagious Diseases Act should be amended in such a way that farmers who have an infected herd would be required to dispose of their herd entirely, and the federal government should exempt those farmers from income tax for a period so that they could restock their herd. Further, a farmer should be required to restock only after a waiting period of one year, under the supervision of the health of animals branch, and compensation for cow and calf should be in line with the replacement value plus one calf crop for one year.
I might add that I have received many letters from farmers who have been asked to dispose of their cattle because of Bang's disease. On the average they have been receiving around $200 for a cow at the stockyard. Further, they receive on the average about $100 in compensation. It works out to an average figure of $300 per animal. When a farmer buys a cow, he must pay $400 to $450 on the open market. Since the farmer probably has lost a cow which has been aborted, he has also lost a calf which would be valued at between $100 and $200. These farmers feel the compensation should be considerably higher than it is, and that it should be equivalent to the replacement value.
The Canadian producers in our area, and I would say throughout northern Saskatchewan or any area in Canada which is affected, feel there should be a little more provincial-federal co-operation in respect of the control of brucellosis and that, particularly, there should be more stringent action regarding disinfecting stations. The farmer who sells diseased animals to the stockyards should have access to proper disinfecting equipment. I understand that in many cases they do not have access to such equipment.
There should be more stringent regulation of community pastures. The farmers also feel that where there is any possibility of infection, or where animals have been in a community pasture and have had Bang's disease, there

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BRUCELLOSIS-REQUEST THAT COMPENSATION TO FARMERS BE EQUATED WITH FAIR MARKET VALUE-SUGGESTED VACCINATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member referred to the level of compensation payable under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. The problem is under very careful study, and it is hoped that there will be a statement on this matter soon.
The number of reactors to this disease, in Saskatchewan, are as follows:
1966-67	889 cases
1967-68	711 cases
1968-69	389 cases
1969-70	885 cases
1970-71	1078 cases
1971-72	2033 cases
1972-73	2544 cases
For 1973-1974, 1109 reactors have been found to date. The situation is under constant surveillance, by the department's Health of Animals Branch.
At this point, I should perhaps mention that there are two justifications for this increase. First, the slaughter of entire herds when there is evidence of a large number of reactors. As the herds increase in size, the number of reactors follows suit.
The incidence of the disease has increased in the north of Saskatchewan. The department has intensified surveillance and testing in cattle enclosures, auctions, etc., and is doing everything possible to have animals identified as reactors slaughtered as quickly as possible. An extra official has been sent to the area to help implement the checking program.
The hon. member spoke of vaccine; I should like to mention that there is an available vaccine for calves. However, it is not 100 per cent efficient and it interferes with the testing program, since it is impossible to distinguish between animals that have been vaccinated and those that have been infected naturally.

As regards cases of the disease in human beings, the Health of Animals Branch gets its information from officials of the provincial health units.
For Saskatchewan, three cases were reported in 1967, three in 1968, one in 1969, two in 1970, one in 1971, and four in 1972.
The Saskatchewan Department of Public Health stated that it had not yet obtained statistics for 1973.

subtopic: HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-POSSIBLE USE AFTER FORECLOSURE
HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-POSSIBLE USE AFTER FORECLOSURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his attendance tonight. This subject was discussed last week in one of the adjournment debates and a statement was made by the parliamentary secretary that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) wrote on April 13, over a month ago, to the metro police commission chairman and to the attorney general of the province of Ontario setting out the federal position respecting Rochdale, and offering full co-operation in the attorney general's proposed investigation of that institution. He asked for the consent of hon. members to table copies of the minister's letter at that time.
I called Sessional Papers this afternoon asking for a copy of that tabled letter, but was told that it had not been received because it was contrary to the rules for any documents to be tabled during these adjournment debates. That being the case, Mr. Speaker, I would welcome a copy of the minister's letter if I could receive it in some other way.
Recently at Rochdale college in Toronto a young man in my constituency met a tragic death. Nothing can be done to restore him, but something must be done to prevent this tragedy being repeated. Rochdale college should become a place in which the public can believe and of which it would not be ashamed. It was erected as an institution for free education; it has become a supermarket for drugs. The government has been urged many times to put this government-financed building to better use, but it has been slow to act. Perhaps it has been reluctant to admit it made a mistake in the first place when it funded the construction of Rochdale and then subsidized it with LIP and OFY grants. Whatever the reason, it has been slow to act.
The government has begun foreclosure proceedings in the courts. It has appointed a management receiver to supervise administration. But such steps are not enough. While foreclosure proceedings drag on, the drug traffic continues. While the receiver makes his efforts at reform, violence still reigns. A report on police activity at Rochdale shows how sordid a record this social monstrosity has. This report tells of drug trafficking so extensive that since January 1, 1973, 379 persons have been charged with drug and narcotic offences, 100 have been charged with trafficking and seizures have been made ranging up to 450 pounds of marijuana. Other offences have included robbery, dangerous weapons, thefts, obstructing and assaulting police, harbouring criminals, dangerous driving, driving under suspension, and even one case of murder.
May 22, 1973

J. S. Boldizar, vice-president of Rochdale, is reported in the press as saying that as many as eight major drug suppliers and 75 dealers operated in Rochdale last summer. The receiver has recently announced that drug traffickers and users must go. This action is welcome, but in many ways it is too little and too late.
I urge the minister to take an action on which I have sought legal advice. Let him, through the management receiver, take over full authority for this building. Let him appoint new administrators. Let him clear out the present tenants. Let him replace them with other citizens who will devote this building to a decent and useful purpose. It could be a home for senior citizens. It could be an apartment house for low-income earners. Every week I receive appeals from pensioners who now have to wait up to two years for public housing because the need is so great. Every week I receive appeals from low-income earners whose names are at the bottom of an Ontario Housing waiting list 17,000 names long.
The minister may defend his policy of doing little and as late as possible, but the people of Canada cannot take him seriously if he says they have put about $5 million into a building and yet must allow it to be abused this way. The management receiver is said to have told the Rochdale college council that his firm had no mandate to clear out the building. I urge the minister to give the receivers that mandate and tell them to act on it.
Rochdale is reported to be more than $1,375,000 behind in mortgage and tax payments. Over $150,000 in collected rent is said to have disappeared in five years. What home owner, struggling to pay his mortgage and his taxes, could get away with that? When representatives of the government tell us that the law forces us to tolerate this, the ordinary citizen must conclude that Mr. Bumble was right and the law really is an ass.
I urge the minister to take an action that the law will permit-to take over the management of Rochdale college and devote it to a purpose the public can support. Threats of riot and mayhem must be rejected. We have been told that there would be a bloodbath, that there would be chaos if the government moved in this direction. But if a group can blackmail a government with that kind of threat, we no longer have a government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-ROCHDALE COLLEGE-POSSIBLE USE AFTER FORECLOSURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the hon. member with some dismay because this analysis of the situation, with all due respect, comes from a person who is either being deliberately mischievous, ignorant or grossly stupid. When the hon. member suggests that the government should do this or that, and that the minister should tell the receiver manager to do this, that or the other, I would like to put the facts on the record.
The fact of the matter is that the position of the Government of Canada with regard to Rochdale is simply that of anyone who has lent money on a mortgage. That mortgage is in default and CMHC has acted as quickly as the law
Adjournment Debate
allows. We have to live within the law-I think even the hon. member would agree with that-and the government has proceeded within the law to secure its rights under that mortgage with all the expedition that the law allows. It commenced foreclosure proceedings on August 17, 1971. At that time it sought in the courts of Ontario interim possession and interim receivership of the building, and was refused by the courts.
If the hon. member is telling me that in spite of that court order which refused Central Mortgage and Housing, refused the Government of Canada possession of the building, the government should take possession illegally, then he is very ignorant or is being very mischievous. Having failed through the courts to get interim receivership or interim management of the building, we took unusual and novel proceedings, which have worked, by applying to the courts for the appointment of a court appointed receiver, not for Central Mortgage and Housing but for all of the creditors. That was granted and on September 1, 1972, the Clarkson company was appointed by the courts as interim receiver and manager of the building.
That receiver accounts, not to me, not to Central Mortgage and Housing but to the Ontario Supreme Court. He reports to the court and is under orders of the court. On the basis of Friday's press release, I think he is making progress in cleaning up the situation in Rochdale. In the meantime, Central Mortgage and Housing and its solicitors, under my instructions, are proceeding as expeditiously as the law allows to prosecute its foreclosure proceedings. I hope they will be set down for trial as early as possible.
I hope the Chief Justice of Ontario, who is responsible for placing matters on the trial list, will see that the action of Central Mortgage and Housing on foreclosure receives an early trial and is handled expeditiously in the Supreme Court of Ontario. That is not under my control. As the hon. member knows, the setting of the trial date is a court proceeding in itself. However, I hope it would not be improper of me to suggest, in regard to these proceedings, that the Chief Justice take note of their special nature and the need for the protection of the interests of the taxpayer and give this matter an early trial.
In the meantime, if the hon. member and his colleagues want to continue making political hay out of this situation in which the government is acting as fast as the law allows, he should use his political influence to get an answer to the letter he mentioned which was written to the chairman of the metropolitan board of police commissioners, and send a copy to the attorney general of Ontario asking for co-operation. He might get a reply to that letter from his Conservative colleagues in Ontario. It has not been replied to as yet. If the hon. gentleman wants to make political hay, I will meet him on these grounds. But he is rather silly to be urging the government to take action that the courts of Ontario have specifically barred it from taking.
